docs.title: 🧩 Plugins Tab (plugin-settings)
docs.text:
settings/plugin-settings.spec.ts drives Settings › Plugins and Configure on the lane's real backend, on desktop only: its member and administrator tests write mockprov fields, one account each, which a second Playwright project would share. Each check reads test ids, data-* attributes, the app events of notify() and the API, never a translated text. mockprov is test-only, so the tab never lists it: the tests reach it the way a user reaches a provider already assigned, from the edit dialog of an asset of their own, assigned mockprov over the API.

Test What it checks Read only, as a member and as an administrator ?tab=plugins selects the tab and its read settles (data-busy); the price family lists justETF and Borsa Italiana, configured, each personal select on its default and editable, with the options the plugin declares (preferred_currency: all, EUR, USD, CHF, GBP; preferred_language: all, it, en), opened and closed with Escape, nothing saved; mockprov never listed A member, through Configure The four instance fields read only (adminOnly), the instance secret only set or unset; results_limit and a personal secret saved — the PATCH sends the number as a number and the secret only in secret_value, and pluginSettings.saved names the fields, never a value — then read back, the API never returning the secret; then Use the default and Clear, saved, back to the default and unset An administrator, through Configure mockprov's instance api_key saved and never shown again (Replace opens an empty field, then cancelled), then cleared Search On a simulated stream (page.route), justETF reported NOT_CONFIGURED gets its «to configure» row and a 👑 result brings the legend; the row's Configure opens justETF's settings over the asset dialog, closed without saving

Every mockprov field a test may write is recorded before its Save and cleared over the API by the account that wrote it after each test, whatever happened; then the asset is deleted. Prerequisites: the test users (e2e_test_user a member, e2e_test_admin an administrator); no environment variable sets a mockprov field on the lane (LIBREFOLIO_MOCKPROV_API_KEY, LIBREFOLIO_PLUGIN_ASSET_MOCKPROV_*); the justETF and Borsa Italiana search preferences of both users on their default. The tab's rules without a browser are in the Vitest files listed in Plugin Settings › Tests. Run it alone with ./dev.py test front-utility plugin-settings.

docs.title: 🛡️ CSP Collector (csp-collector)
docs.text:
layout/csp-collector.spec.ts tests the CSP collector that every spec carries, with service workers blocked so that every document goes through the spec's own routes. It runs on any lane. The spec computes the managed profile's report-only policy itself, with its own HTML reader and Node's crypto: its copy of CSP_REPORT_ONLY_POLICY, with the hashes of the inline scripts of /, /200.html and /offline.html as the lane serves them. On a self-hosted lane it adds that policy to the app's pages; on a managed one it lets the lane's own header through and requires it to equal its own, to the letter, on every page of the build.

Test What it checks The pure logic cspCollectorEnabled, isKnown and loadBaseline of e2e/fixtures/csp.ts, on synthetic input, without a page: an entry known by its directive and blocked URI on any line (no line span any more); an address known by its path, whole, whatever its origin and query, and a blocked URI that is no absolute URL (inline, eval) never known by a path; an entry with a sample knowing only that exact sample, an entry without one ignoring it; every entry of the baseline well formed (exactly one of blockedURI and blockedPath, a sample only when not empty, a reason, an owner, no other key), every id its own The first cloud smoke's findings The real baseline knows them as the managed lane recorded them, cheetah-grid's global probe by its exact sample and three address checks of a link by their path, each by the entry recorded for it and by no other; an eval of other code, and the probe without a sample, stay unknown The spec's own reading On synthetic input, what it checks the backend with: the text of every inline script, of any type (none in a comment, a <title> or a <style>), its sha256 source (against CSP Level 2's published example, CR LF and a lone CR hashed as LF), every inline event-handler attribute, and the policy built from the hashes, each once, sorted, after 'report-sample' A synthetic document Served by the spec under its own report-only script-src 'self': its inline script recorded once, field for field as the page saw it, and run all the same; unknown, and the test passes (cspFailOnUnknown: false) Two documents in a row A navigation: the violations of both recorded, the binding and the listener back with each document An unknown violation With cspFailOnUnknown at its default, the test fails at teardown: an expected failure (test.fail()), which Playwright reports passed only if it did fail The sign-in page / under that policy reports no violation at all, as the page and the collector both saw it. Then a control, a script of the lane's origin that probes the global object as cheetah-grid does, is reported with that probe's exact sample and known by cheetah-grid-global-probe alone: the silence was measured. Under JS coverage, istanbul's own probes are left out The offline page /offline.html under the same policy loads with no violation, its script allowed by its hash; no page of the build has an inline event-handler attribute; its retry button loads it again, with no violation either The kill switch Runs only in a run started with E2E_CSP_COLLECTOR=0, where the tests on synthetic documents and on the app's pages skip: no binding in the page, nothing recorded, nothing failed

Prerequisites: populated DB and test users. Run it alone with ./dev.py test front-utility csp-collector, and its kill-switch test with E2E_CSP_COLLECTOR=0 ./dev.py test front-utility csp-collector.

docs.title: ☁️ Cloud Smoke (cloud-smoke)
docs.text:
The main pages and the surfaces the managed profile's policies touch (the PDF preview, forms, frames), on a managed lane: frame protection and the report-only policy for real, with the CSP collector failing on any violation e2e/csp-baseline.json does not know. Thirteen specs of the suite, CLOUD_SMOKE_SPECS in scripts/test_runner/_frontend_utility.py, on desktop only (each <name>.spec.ts under frontend/e2e/): auth, layout/page-policy, layout/csp-collector, portfolio/dashboard, portfolio/risk-analysis, assets/asset-modal, transactions/transactions-table, transactions/tx-brim-import, files, brokers/brokers, settings/security-tab, settings/admin-users and ai-export/ai-export-panel. layout/legal-and-managed stays out until its tests of the lane's own answer (LGM-E-01, LGM-E-03) read the lane's profile: they pin a self-hosted lane, and fail on a managed one by design.

On any lane it runs only when named: registered named_only=True, it is left out of front-utility all, all-frontend and all, their consolidated pass included (see Registry Entry Shape). It refuses to start unless the lane's LIBREFOLIO_PROFILE is managed, with an error that says to add --lane-setting LIBREFOLIO_PROFILE=managed, a flag of ./dev.py test that goes before the category (see Lane Settings). Prerequisites: that lane, a populated DB and the test users.

docs.title: 🏗️ Test Runner Architecture
docs.text: This document describes the design and inner workings of the modular test orchestrator located in scripts/test_runner/.

docs.title: 🏗️ Architecture Overview
docs.text:
LibreFolio orchestrates its test execution through a custom Python package rather than a static, monolithic script. The package separates what exists from how it is grouped from how it is run — three concerns that used to live inside a single function per test action, which is why parallel execution was impossible before.

---
config:
  layout: elk
---
graph TD
    DEV["./dev.py test ..."] -->|1. Invokes| CLI["_cli.py"]
    CLI -->|2. Imports| REG["_registry.py"]
    REG -->|3. Dynamically populates| TEST_REG["TEST_REGISTRY Map"]

    subgraph Test Suite Modules [Test Categories]
        direction LR
        BE["_backend_*.py<br/><small>db, services, api, etc.</small>"]
        FE["_frontend_*.py<br/><small>asset, fx, transaction, etc.</small>"]
    end

    BE -.->|registers| TEST_REG
    FE -.->|registers| TEST_REG

    TEST_REG -->|4. Collected without running| INV["_inventory.py<br/><small>test units + isolation class</small>"]
    INV -->|5. + --workers N| SCHED["_scheduler.py<br/><small>LPT balancing</small>"]
    INV -->|5b. Frontend, grouped| CONS["_consolidate.py<br/><small>one invocation per category</small>"]
    SCHED -->|6. Execution plan| EXEC["_executor.py<br/><small>one process per group</small>"]
    CLI -->|7. Remaining actions| SUITES["_suites.py"]
    SUITES -->|8. Controls coverage| COV["_coverage.py"]
    EXEC -->|9. Spawns| PYT["pytest / Playwright / vitest"]
    CONS -->|9. Spawns| PYT
    SUITES -->|9. Spawns| PYT

docs.title: 🧭 The Inventory (_inventory.py)
docs.text:
The inventory answers one question — what test units exist? — and it answers it by derivation, never by a hand-written list. Hand-written lists drift silently: before the inventory existed, six registered actions covering roughly 259 tests were reachable by name but executed by no all list, and the orphan check could not see it because it grepped for filenames rather than reasoning about reachability.

Collection works because the action functions are almost-pure command producers. Replacing run_command and _run_playwright with collectors makes every action report what it would launch without launching anything, so the whole registry can be inspected in well under a second.

Two actions do real work during collection

db create and db populate do not merely compose a command — db create calls TEST_DB_PATH.unlink() for real, and an early collection pass genuinely emptied the test database. They are therefore neutralised both in the registry dictionary and in the module that defines them, because the all suites hold direct references to the function object. A guard on Path.unlink during collection catches any future action that acquires the same habit.

docs.title: Isolation classes
docs.text:
Every unit carries the class that says what it needs in order not to disturb anything else. The classes come from the data model: of the 12 tables only UserSettings and BrokerUserAccess are per-user, so almost every write lands on a shared surface.

Class Meaning Can share with… Dedicated resource PURE touches neither the database nor a server anything COVERAGE_FILE only READ reads shared data, never writes other READs, on one backend none WRITE-SCOPED writes only rows owned by its own user/broker other WRITE-SCOPED with a different user one E2E user WRITE-GLOBAL writes shared surfaces (assets, FX, prices, settings) nothing a whole database

Classification is deliberately strict: vitest units are PURE by construction, a pytest unit is PURE only when neither the file nor the helpers it imports mention a shared-state marker, and everything else falls through to WRITE-GLOBAL. The asymmetry is the point — a wrong PURE produces an intermittent red, while a wrong WRITE-GLOBAL only costs time.

Impurity travels through imports

A test file can look spotless and still import test_db_config, which points at the shared test database. Classification therefore follows test_utils, test_db_config and test_server_helper one level deep. One level is enough because those helpers do not import each other.

READ and WRITE-SCOPED must be declared before they can be trusted; a textual heuristic was tried and misclassified real cases, so until a unit is declared it stays serial.

docs.title: Declaring a class — and earning it
docs.text:
The default is correct but it is not free: left alone, it serialised 50 of the 51 api units and 37 of the 85 services units for no reason at all. The debt was never in the tests — it was in the catalogue, which had no way to be told it was wrong.

Declare per unit, or on the category when the property holds for all of it:

make_category(
    "api", ...,
    # every unit creates its own user and addresses its own rows by id
    default_isolation="write-scoped",
)

add_test(
    "auth", ...,
    exclusive_because="rewrites global_settings.registration_mode, one row shared by every user: "
                      "a concurrent unit would register against whatever value this one left behind",
)

exclusive_because is the WRITE-GLOBAL declaration, not a comment next to a flag. Storing the class and its justification as one statement means a category default cannot silently promote a unit somebody already explained must not be promoted — and the catalogue of exceptions is generated rather than maintained by hand.

A class claim is earned by a passing parallel run, not asserted

--assume-scoped ignores the catalogue and runs everything concurrently. Use it once per category to find out what the catalogue was getting wrong, read the reds with the test-triage skill, then write down what you learnt. It is experiment instrumentation, never a default.

On api that experiment produced 14 reds out of 603 tests, thirteen of which had a single cause: test_auth_api.py turning registration off while its neighbours were creating users. The fourteenth had nothing to do with concurrency — it reached the real ECB over the internet.

docs.title: How to ask for an exclusive, and what justifies one
docs.text:
The whole backend currently has one exclusive unit. That number is the point of the section: it is small because an exclusive has to survive being written down.

Unit Why it cannot be scoped api auth rewrites global_settings.registration_mode — one row shared by every user, not a per-user row. A concurrent unit would register against whatever value this one left behind (disabled while it checks closed registration), and a test that verifies a registration mode on the lane's server necessarily owns the instance.

The units that came with the registration modes show the other way out: api registration and api users-admin run every case that needs another mode, an accounts variable or a user limit in-process, on a private database, and touch only their own accounts and tokens on the lane's server, so they stay WRITE-SCOPED with no exclusive. api admin-setup goes the same way: an administrator waiting for its setup exists only on an instance that had no account, so every case that needs one runs in-process on a private database, and the lane's server only gets refusals that write nothing.

Two claims that look like reasons and are not:

  • "It reaches a third party over the network, so it is slow and fragile." That is a reason to stop reaching the third party, not to take the database. api fx held an exclusive on exactly this argument until the three syncs were pointed at MOCKFX; it now runs with everyone else, and its assertions became exact in the process.
  • "It failed when I ran it in parallel." Say what it mutates. If you cannot name the shared surface, the cause is somewhere else — read the reds with the test-triage skill first, because the loudest failure is usually not the one doing the damage.

The test is simple: name the surface, and say why it has no per-user equivalent. If the sentence works, it belongs in exclusive_because and the exclusive is granted by the same act. If it does not, the unit is not exclusive — it is unfinished.

docs.title: 🧹 Shared state: whoever commits, cleans up
docs.text: This is a rule for whoever writes the next test, not an implementation note. It is the one thing in this page you can break without any tool telling you.

docs.title: Why the old design hid the problem
docs.text:
While the runner spent one process per action, every test file effectively got a fresh database: globalSetup re-populated before each Playwright invocation, and each pytest invocation started from a clean import. A test could write whatever it liked and walk away — the evidence was wiped before anyone could trip over it.

Consolidation removes that accident. Once several units share one invocation, what one leaves behind becomes the next one's input. No test changed; the contract they were all silently relying on did.

docs.title: The rule
docs.text:
A test that commits to a shared surface must restore it, in its own teardown, without assuming a freshly populated database.

"Shared surface" is almost everything: of 12 tables only UserSettings and BrokerUserAccess are per-user. Transaction in particular has no user_id — isolation happens at service level via broker access — so a committed transaction is visible to every later test.

Tests that only read, and fixtures that flush and roll back, are already compliant and need nothing. The only candidates are fixtures and specs that deliberately call commit() — few, and findable.

docs.title: Backend
docs.text:
@pytest_asyncio.fixture(scope="module")
async def fx_asset_ids():
    ...                       # writes and commits
    yield asset_id
    async with ... as session:   # and now puts it back
        await session.execute(delete(PriceHistory).where(...))
        await session.execute(delete(FxRate).where(...))
        await session.execute(delete(Asset).where(Asset.id == asset_id))
        await session.commit()

Without that teardown the committed FX rows collide with a later session.add() on the same (date, base, quote) key, and the failure surfaces in a different file — which is what makes this class of bug expensive.

docs.title: Frontend (E2E)
docs.text:
An E2E test writes over HTTP, so there is no session to roll back. Use trackTransactionWrites() from frontend/e2e/fixtures/db-cleanup.ts: it records the transactions that this page's own commits created, and its cleanup() deletes exactly those.

import {trackTransactionWrites, type TransactionWriteTracker} from '../fixtures/db-cleanup';

let txWrites: TransactionWriteTracker | undefined;

test.beforeEach(async ({page}) => {
    await login(page, TEST_USER);
    // After login (it reads through page.request, which needs the session cookie), before any commit.
    txWrites = await trackTransactionWrites(page);
    await goToTransactions(page);
});

test.afterEach(async () => {
    await txWrites?.cleanup();   // afterEach runs for a red test too
});

A row is the test's own only when two facts agree: a committed POST /transactions/commit made by this page reported its id as created (a create, split or promote result), and the id was not in the snapshot trackTransactionWrites() took when it started. The commit response lists the rows created indirectly too — the second half of a linked pair, a promoted transfer — so the spec never has to name them; the snapshot keeps a split or a promote of fixture data from deleting the fixture row it came from. cleanup() skips the ids already gone (deleting one half of a linked pair removes both) and throws when the delete request fails.

Never delete whatever is new since a snapshot

The first version of this helper did exactly that: photograph before, delete what appeared after. It reads "new" as "mine", which holds only while nothing else runs at the same time — the reason the txHygiene fixture below works only at one worker. Under concurrent workers the rows a neighbour is still using are new too, and the helper deleted them, or failed with a 500 on a row the neighbour had already removed.

A test that commits rows nobody else should see can also work on an account of its own: openOwnedAccount() and openAccountWithPair() in frontend/e2e/fixtures/owned-pair.ts register a disposable account, and cleanupOwnedAccount() deletes its brokers — their transactions go with them — and then the account.

The bug this rule was written from

tx-clone.spec.ts cloned "the first paired giver row on editable brokers" and committed it for real. That row was the delete-safe ETH transfer. tx-delete.spec.ts then deleted that pair and asserted nothing matching survived — and found the clone. Neither test was wrong; the implicit contract between them was. Both sides have since been fixed: tx-clone commits only onto a broker or an account of its own and deletes what it commits, and tx-delete deletes only rows it creates.

docs.title: --workers reaches Playwright too
docs.text:
The frontend has two worker counts, and they are derived from the same number:

./dev.py test front-transaction --workers 4
        │
        ├─ shared_backend_for → SharedTestServer: max(1, ⌈4 / 2⌉) = 2      (uvicorn processes)
        │                         └─ playwright.config.ts reuses it instead of starting its own
        │
        └─ _apply_parallel  → _common._E2E_WORKERS = 4
                                └─ apply_e2e_workers: min(4, max(1, ⌊logical cores / 2⌋)) → E2E_WORKERS
                                     └─ playwright.config.ts: workers: E2E_WORKERS   (browser contexts)

apply_e2e_workers(), which both Playwright launches call (per unit and consolidated), caps the browser workers at half the logical cores, never below one: --workers 4 gives four from 8 logical cores up. It exports E2E_WORKERS only when the result is above 1 and the variable is not already set; otherwise playwright.config.ts runs what the environment says, or 1.

Under the runner the backend is the shared one (SharedTestServer), which Playwright reuses, and it is sized from --workers itself, before that cap: one uvicorn worker per two, rounded up (1 → 1, 3 → 2, 4 → 2). --workers 8 on 10 logical cores therefore runs 5 browser workers against 4 uvicorn workers. playwright.config.ts sizes a backend only when it starts one itself — with --no-shared-server, for the gallery, or with npx playwright test by hand — by the same rule applied to the browser count: SERVER_WORKERS = max(1, ⌈E2E_WORKERS / 2⌉), unless LIBREFOLIO_SERVER_WORKERS or, failing that, GALLERY_SERVER_WORKERS (the gallery's one per four) sets it. The ratio is deliberate, and _server.py gives the reason (CLIENTS_PER_SERVER_WORKER): API and E2E workers hit the backend hard, hence one uvicorn worker per two of them, while the gallery's one per four rests on its browser workers spending most of their time rendering. A suite that never makes the backend queue is not testing concurrency, it is only testing itself faster.

The environment variable is not the interface

E2E_WORKERS existed long before --workers wrote it. That gap meant ./dev.py test front-transaction --workers 4 gave four uvicorn workers and one browser worker: the flag was half-obeyed, silently. If you set E2E_WORKERS in your shell it still wins, uncapped — the runner does not overwrite a value you chose deliberately. The shared backend is still sized from --workers, not from that value.

Do not edit the repository while an E2E run is in flight

Under the runner the backend is started by SharedTestServer; Playwright's own webServer starts one only when no shared backend is up — with --no-shared-server, for the gallery, or with npx playwright test by hand. Either way it must be started with --no-reload — found the hard way — and both paths pass it, together with --no-scheduler. Under --reload uvicorn watches the repo root: a single saved file restarts the backend mid-run, and every test that happens to be logging in at that moment dies at 20 s. The signature is unmistakable — a burst of login() timeouts in the tests scheduled first, scattered across unrelated files. It reads exactly like a concurrency bug, and it is not one.

docs.title: 🧮 The Scheduler (_scheduler.py)
docs.text:
The scheduler turns inventory + --workers N into an execution plan. It decides what runs with what using the isolation class alone — never a test name or a directory shape.

Balancing is longest-processing-time first: the longest unit goes to the currently shortest group. Round-robin was measured losing about half the theoretical gain, because one group finished in 32 s while another was still running at 84 s and the run is only as fast as its slowest group. Durations come from the workers' JUnit reports and are persisted in .coverage_data/unit_durations.json, so the first run balances on a median guess and every run after that balances on measurement.

An action is marked as already covered — and therefore skipped in the serial pass — only when every path it launches is in the parallel set. A mixed action would otherwise lose its WRITE-GLOBAL half in silence.

docs.title: ⚙️ The Executor (_executor.py)
docs.text:
Each group runs in its own process with an exclusive lot of resources. Today the lot holds one item, COVERAGE_FILE, because only PURE units are parallelised and they need nothing else; the database, the port and the E2E user join the lot as the write classes are activated.

Resource Serial Per worker Needed by COVERAGE_FILE global .coverage, copied in and out .coverage_data/parts/run-<YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS>-<pid>/.coverage.p<pass>.wN every worker DATABASE_URL one shared app.db app_wN.db WRITE-GLOBAL TEST_PORT fixed TEST_PORT + N backend workers with an in-process server E2E user always e2e_test_user one of the eight WRITE-SCOPED

Workers also run with -p no:cacheprovider and without --cov-report, since a shared .pytest_cache and a shared htmlcov-backend/ would be written by every worker at once.

Failure policy: stop assigning, never kill

By default the run continues past a red and reports the full list. Under --fail-fast the scheduler hands out no further work, but workers already running are still left to finish: killing a worker mid-flight discards its coverage, and coverage that disappears without failing is the most expensive defect this project has met.

docs.title: --workers
docs.text:
• --workers 1 (default) is the serial path, not an approximation of it: the plan has one group and execution follows exactly the route it followed before the migration.
  • --workers N parallelises the isolation-safe units and leaves everything else serial — a WRITE-GLOBAL unit stays serial even at --workers 8.
  • The parallel pass plans category by category, so it runs only for a whole backend category (<category> all) or a whole suite (all, all-backend): naming one action, or filtering by test name (pytest -k, which only a named action takes), keeps the serial path. The check is _parallel_prepass_applies(), which follows the same scope rule as the consolidated pre-passes (_backend_consolidation_scope()).
  • --workers auto resolves to half the cores, because a development machine is not dedicated to tests and timing-sensitive tests degrade under load.
  • On a frontend category the same flag sets Playwright's browser workers, capped at half the logical cores, and the number of uvicorn processes behind them — the shared backend is sized from the flag itself, not from the capped count (see --workers reaches Playwright too).

The flag belongs to ./dev.py test, so it goes before the category:

./dev.py test --workers 4 services all
./dev.py test --workers auto --coverage py all-backend

Measured on utils all: 258 tests in 31.8 s serially, the same 258 tests in 22.8 s at four workers, with an identical coverage total of 14.73 %. On services all the parallel pass ran 44 units and 1329 tests in 41.5 s.

docs.title: What the whole backend actually gains
docs.text:
all-backend with coverage, run both ways from a clean database:

--workers 1 --workers 4 Tests 4654 4654 Failures 0 0 Coverage 37336 stmts / 3224 missing / 91.36 % 37336 / 3224 / 91.36 % Wall time 38 min 52 s 31 min 03 s

The coverage figures are identical digit for digit, and identical file by file across all 241 modules — the only check worth making on a tool that can silently lose data. The speedup — 1.25× — is deliberately modest: the parallel pass finishes 51 PURE units (1494 tests) in 32.2 s with workers landing at 32.2 / 32.1 / 32.1 / 32.1 s, so the LPT balancing is close to perfect, but everything else is WRITE-GLOBAL and stays serial by design. Going further means one database per worker, not a bigger N.

The total has a noise floor of about 4 statements — and it is attributable

Two runs launched minutes apart matched exactly. A third, hours later, closed at 3220 uncovered instead of 3224 — more covered, despite doing strictly less work, which is causally impossible for a deterministic number.

Compared file by file, the difference sits entirely in the asset pricing service (a single module at the time, now split across the backend/app/services/assets/ package) and asset_source_providers/borsa_italiana/plugin.py: the two places that talk to the live internet. Test and skip counts were identical in all three runs, so nothing changed about what ran — only which branch the provider took given what the site returned that day.

So compare per file, not on the total. On the total, 4 statements of network noise are indistinguishable from a real loss of data; per file they are immediately attributable.

A running test server poisons the whole backend run

--fresh-run starts with db create, which unlinks the database first and only then calls db:upgrade — and db:upgrade refuses to migrate while something holds the lane's test port (TEST_PORT, 6041 by default). The result is not one clear error but roughly a dozen unrelated-looking reds downstream, all caused by a database that no longer exists. Check lsof -ti:6041 (or your lane's port) is empty before a backend run.

docs.title: On failure
docs.text:
By default every unit runs and every failure is reported, across the parallel pass, the consolidation pass and the serial suite. The reason is empirical: reds arrive in clusters, and nine failures in one worker are usually nine symptoms of one cause — a list you cannot see if the run stops at the first, and that costs one full re-run per red to rediscover.

--fail-fast inverts it: the scheduler hands out no further work and the serial pass stops at the failing action. Workers already started are still left to finish their batch — killing one mid-flight would discard its coverage, which is exactly how P7 lost data without anything turning red.

docs.title: 📦 Frontend consolidation (_consolidate.py)
docs.text:
On the backend the win is parallelism. On the frontend it is not invoking Playwright 120 times.

Each frontend action used to pay, before running a single assertion: a database populate, eight user creations, a globalSetup that populates and creates users again, and a webServer start/stop — roughly eleven cold Python starts per spec file. Measured on front-fx: seven invocations run 42 tests in 502.6 s, while one invocation runs those same 42 tests plus 21 more in 218.6 s.

So the units of a category are grouped into one Playwright invocation and one vitest invocation:

Category Playwright vitest invocations before after front-ai-export 4 22 26 2 front-asset 7 15 22 2 front-broker 2 3 5 2 front-designer-lab 3 15 18 2 front-fx 8 3 11 2 front-portfolio 3 3 6 2 front-transaction 25 7 32 2 front-user 2 2 4 2 front-utility 8 6 14 2 total 62 76 138 18

The after column is the shape without JS coverage. With --coverage js the Playwright side is run in batches of 8 specs (see below), so front-transaction costs 4 invocations instead of 1 and the total is 23 rather than 18.

Consolidation is now also what makes parallelism possible

The startup saving above was the original reason. Since fullyParallel: true, there is a second one that matters more: a Playwright invocation can only distribute the tests it was given. One spec file per invocation means one unit of work, and --workers 4 buys nothing at all — three browsers sit idle. Consolidation is what turns a category into a pool the scheduler can spread. On front-transaction the two effects are not comparable: grouping alone was worth ~0,2 min, grouping plus four workers is worth 11.

docs.title: A long-lived worker exposes what a short-lived one hid
docs.text:
Grouping changes the lifetime of the process, and anything that accumulated per test used to be collected for free when the process died after one spec file. It no longer is.

The case that bit: with --coverage js, the fixture called MCR(options) — a constructor, not a singleton — once per test, and each instance re-resolved the sourcemaps of the whole build. Worse, monocart's add() writes its payload to the cache directory and keeps a copy in an instance-level Map, keyed by a fresh id per call. That map is an optimisation for callers that add() and generate() in one process; here the fixture only adds, and scripts/mcr-generate.js produces the report later in a different process, reading the same data back from disk. Every retained entry was a complete V8 payload — sources and sourcemaps — kept for a reader that never looks.

Over one spec file, invisible. Over 25, the worker died at the heap limit.

Both were real and both were fixed — a worker-scoped mcr fixture, and fileCache.clear() after each add(). Neither made the crash go away. Each one bought about four minutes:

Configuration Ceiling Reached after 25 specs, MCR per test, default heap ~4 GB ~700 s 25 specs, one MCR per worker, --max-old-space-size=8192 8181 MB 988 s 25 specs, and fileCache.clear() 8174 MB 1214 s 8 specs, same two fixes — no OOM, 163 tests green in 7.8 min

The last row is the one that settles it: with identical code, a group of 8 finishes and a group of 25 does not. The quantity that matters is not what any single test does, it is how long the process lives. So the answer is a scheduling decision, not another hunt through monocart: with JS coverage on, a group is run in batches of 8 specs (_JS_COVERAGE_CHUNK). front-transaction goes from 25 invocations to 4 rather than to 1 — about a minute and a half of extra globalSetup in total, against a run that previously never reached the end.

The crash was also falsifying the measurement, which is the part worth remembering. A full --coverage all --workers 4 all run before the fix reported 91.38 % Python coverage; after it, doing exactly the same work, it reports 91.64 % — 98 more statements. The specs that died of OOM were exercising the backend through the E2E path, and their coverage vanished with the process. A defect that shows up as slightly lower coverage rather than as an error is the hardest kind to notice: compare the numbers, never the colour.

An out-of-memory worker names the wrong test

Playwright reports it as worker process exited unexpectedly (code=null, signal=SIGABRT) against whichever test was running, with a duration of 0ms. The real message is further up the log: FATAL ERROR: Ineffective mark-compacts near heap limit. A 0ms failure is never an assertion — always look for the crash above it.

Raising --max-old-space-size defers, it does not fix. If a run under JS coverage starts dying again, lower _JS_COVERAGE_CHUNK before raising the heap: bounding the lifetime is the lever that actually works.

The general rule for anything in a consolidated fixture: hold per-worker state deliberately, and release per-test state explicitly. What used to be freed by process death now has to be freed on purpose.

docs.title: The setup runs once, not once per invocation
docs.text:
Even 16 invocations would each redo the same preparation, so the Python side signals that it is already done with LF_SETUP_DONE=1. global-setup.ts then skips populating the database and creating the E2E users, and jumps straight to initialising the global settings via the API — the one step nothing on the Python side performs (populate writes a single row, registration_mode), and one that populate --force wipes.

The variable is set only after both the populate and the users have succeeded, and cleared by any repopulate. Running npx playwright test by hand never has it, so that path is unchanged.

Deduplicate only what is genuinely duplicated

global-setup.ts populated with --with-reports (the sample BRIM files) while the Python _ensure_db_populated() did not. While the JS side redid everything, the difference was invisible — the richer populate simply happened second. Skipping it would have silently removed the fixtures the broker import-history specs depend on, turning an unrelated category red. The Python populate was made a superset first.

docs.title: It only applies to a whole category
docs.text: ./dev.py test front-fx fx-list still means one invocation for one spec. Consolidation applies to all of a category and to all-frontend — the cases where the actions would have run back to back anyway. --no-consolidate, --ui, --headed and --debug all return to the 1:1 shape. Neither all nor all-frontend takes test names: a name after either stops the command with exit code 2.

docs.title: Per-unit outcomes are part of it, not a follow-up
docs.text:
Consolidation on its own would make the runner say "the category is red" instead of naming the spec, and would coarsen --resume from a spec to a category. That is a regression, so the reporters are read back: Playwright and vitest both write a JSON report, and each is folded into a per-spec verdict before anything is printed. The action-level summary stays exactly as detailed as before.

A unit missing from the report counts as failed

Silence must never read as success. That is precisely how a coverage run can drop half its data without anything turning red.

docs.title: The serial suite steps aside when there is nothing left
docs.text:
Once the consolidated pass has run every action of a category, the category's all function returns immediately instead of running the serial route. Without that guard it would still build the frontend, repopulate the database and create the E2E users before discovering it has nothing to execute — about ten seconds per category, and worse than wasteful: the repopulation happens after the consolidated pass, so a log read top-down shows the database being wiped after the tests that used it.

The check is nothing_left_to_run(category) in _common.py, and it is deliberately all-or-nothing: if even one action was left to the serial path, the normal route with its full setup applies.

Stepping aside must not launder a red

A skipped serial suite that returns True makes the category green. The first version of this guard did exactly that, and with the run continuing past the red it printed ✘ front-transaction tx-wac-mode and then, twenty lines below, "🎉 ALL FRONTEND TESTS PASSED! 🎉". The exit code was right the whole time; a summary that contradicts the exit code is worse than no summary.

So the guard returns consolidated_verdict(category), which reports what the pre-pass actually found. _SKIP_ACTIONS and _FAILED_ACTIONS are kept as two separate sets on purpose: they answer "was it already run?" and "did it pass?", and conflating them is precisely how a red becomes a green.

docs.title: The precondition, and how it is met
docs.text:
Consolidated specs share one database, so they must not disturb each other — this is the whoever commits, cleans up rule. In practice the damage is rarely a duplicate key. It is row inflation:

tx-tooltips scans the first 20 rows for an access-test transaction; tx-split-promote looks for a paired row on page one. Neither assertion is wrong. But once earlier specs have added a hundred rows that sort ahead of the fixtures, neither finds what it needs — and the spec that gets blamed is the one that only reads.

Writing beforeEach/afterEach into 59 spec files would work and would be forgotten 59 times, so the guarantee lives in an automatic fixture instead — txHygiene in e2e/fixtures/playwright.ts, next to the JS-coverage one. It photographs the transaction ids when the spec file changes and deletes the difference before the next file starts, through a worker-scoped API context (one login per worker, two calls per file).

Per file, not per test — and the difference is measurable

Cleaning after every test looks tidier and is wrong. When this was measured, specs were written sequentially: tx-commit-all-types committed a BUY and then sold part of it, tx-delete created a pair in one test and deleted it in the next. Wiping between tests broke those chains — tried on the full transactions/ directory, it turned three reds into five. Neither spec chains any more (tx-commit-all-types funds each SELL inside its own batch, and tx-delete deletes only rows it creates), but state may still accumulate inside a file, and the cleanup must not be what breaks it.

What consolidation removed was the inter-file reset: before it, every spec file ran in its own process against a freshly populated database. So that is the invariant to restore, and no more than that. State accumulates freely inside a file and is rolled back when the file changes.

It is active only when LF_TX_HYGIENE=1 and E2E_WORKERS is at most 1 (unset counts as 1). The consolidated pass sets LF_TX_HYGIENE=1, and only when it runs Playwright with one worker. That is deliberate: the invariant "the database is what populate_mock_data produced" needs restoring exactly when specs share it, and someone running a single spec by hand keeps the old path bit for bit. Above one worker, tests from different files interleave against one database: "every id that appeared since this file started" would also cover rows that other workers' tests are still using, and a repopulate would wipe the database under them. So the fixture switches itself off — with a warning, if LF_TX_HYGIENE=1 was set anyway — and each test's own cleanup is all that is left. When the fixture's cleanup fails, it never turns the test red — inventing a red in the innocent spec that happened to run first is worse than the defect being cured.

docs.title: The rollback has to work in both directions
docs.text:
Deleting what a spec added is only half the invariant. A spec that destroys mock rows — tx-delete did, until its confirm tests moved to rows they create on a disposable account — cannot be repaired that way: no API call can bring back a row with its original id and its original half of a linked pair. What followed was a failure that never named the culprit:

tx-picker-pagination alone, fresh database tx-picker-pagination on the database the suite left behind Outcome 5 passed 4 failed

With fewer rows in the table, the spec's first two checkbox clicks landed on a linked pair; the bulk modal treated it as a single entity and opened a form modal by itself; four tests then timed out clicking a button behind that modal's backdrop. The error talked about a tx-form-modal intercepting pointer events and said nothing about tx-delete, which had run earlier in the same pass. It is the same family as row inflation, mirrored: row deflation.

So restore() compares the id set against the opening snapshot. If even one baseline id has gone missing it repopulates, re-initialises the global settings (initGlobalSettings() is exported from global-setup.ts for exactly this) and logs the worker's API context back in — after a repopulate the users have new ids and the session cookie is stale. If nothing is missing it just drops the difference, as before.

A repopulate costs time that belongs to a test

Playwright charges test-scoped fixture setup to the current test's timeout, and these specs run at 25 s. The fixture grants testInfo.setTimeout(+25 s) only when a repopulate actually happened — raising it unconditionally would hide the very slowness those timeouts exist to catch.

Also worth knowing: populate_mock_data recreates the E2E users itself, but of the global settings only one row: registration_mode, written open by open_lane_registration(), since the API and E2E tests register accounts of their own and a new install's default, invite, would refuse them. The other global settings are the one piece of globalSetup that has to be replayed by hand; initGlobalSettings() creates only the missing rows, so it keeps that open.

A wedged test server looks exactly like a hung test suite

An aborted run can leave uvicorn half-shut-down yet still listening on 6041: it accepts connections and answers nothing — /docs and /openapi.json included, so it is the event loop, not a database lock. reuseExistingServer reuses it happily and Playwright parks forever inside globalSetup's fetch, before the reporter has printed a line. The tell is that the Playwright node process has no children and the log stops at the dotenv banner.

Both globalSetup fetches now carry AbortSignal.timeout(20 s) and say what to look for. The cure is to kill the process holding the port and restart with ./dev.py server --test --force.

docs.title: Projects are grouped too
docs.text:
frontend/playwright.config.ts declares two projects: desktop (Desktop Chrome, 1280×720) and mobile (the iPhone 14 Pro Max descriptor, run in Chromium). Outside --ui mode, _run_playwright passes --project desktop unless an action says otherwise, so most actions run on desktop only. An action that passes project="" gets no --project and runs on both: seven front-utility actions (files-uploader, support-copy-and-go, header-scroll, document-title, connection-security, onboarding-tour, onboarding-guides), front-broker broker-create-feedback, front-portfolio privacy-masking, and front-transaction tx-import-report-set and tx-import-report-set-guide. front-ai-export passes project="desktop" explicitly.

So the inventory records the project selector alongside each Playwright unit (ALL_PROJECTS for an action that passes project=""), and consolidation runs one Playwright invocation per (category, project) group (in batches of 8 specs under JS coverage), without --project for the both-project group. Without it, folding those specs into the desktop group would have dropped their mobile run — and, since everything left would still have passed, nothing would have said so.

docs.title: Resuming a consolidated pass
docs.text:
--resume skips units a previous run already passed. The consolidated pass keeps its own run-cache namespace (consolidated:<category>), because the serial suites are indexed by their human title ("Frontend User Tests"), which is written by hand inside each *_all function and cannot be derived from the registry. Guessing it would be fragile; a namespace of our own is exact and obvious in --run-status.

Resumed units still count as covered — the serial pass does not re-run them either.

docs.title: 🗃️ Dynamic Registry Pattern (_registry.py)
docs.text:
To prevent the orchestrator from needing hardcoded knowledge of every single test action, the runner utilizes a Dynamic Registry Pattern.

  1. Central Store: scripts/test_runner/_registry.py defines a global TEST_REGISTRY dictionary.
  2. Registration Hooks: Each test category module (e.g., _backend_utils.py, _frontend_fx.py) implements a populate_registry(registry: dict) function.
  3. Execution Mapping: When the orchestrator starts, it calls the populate functions in order. Each category registers its commands and sub-test functions:
# Example from scripts/test_runner/_backend_utils.py
def populate_registry(registry: dict) -> None:
    cat = make_category(
        help_text="Utility module tests (decimal, datetime, geo, currency, cache)",
        description="Utility Module Tests..."
    )
    # Register actions
    add_test(cat, "decimal-precision", utils_decimal_precision, name="Decimal Precision", desc="...")
    add_test(cat, "all", utils_all, test_names=False, name="All Utils Tests", desc="...")

    registry["utils"] = cat

docs.title: Registry Entry Shape
docs.text:
A category registered in TEST_REGISTRY maps to a dictionary containing:

  • _meta: General information about the category (used for --help texts) and, when the category declares them in make_category(), these keys:
    • setup: What the category does to its environment before its units run: services recreates the test database empty, api reseeds it. run_category_setup() runs it once per invocation, whichever caller reaches it first.
    • setup_exclusive: The setup needs the database file to itself (services), so it is hoisted to before the shared backend starts. For one action run on its own that the catalogue declares pure (as declared_isolation() resolves it: an exclusive_because means write-global, else the action's own isolation, else the category's default_isolation), the setup is skipped, since such a unit opens no database, and one line says the lane's database is left as it is. A whole category, all and any action not declared pure (one with no declared class at all included) still run it. The skip holds at any --workers, since the parallel pass does not run for one action.
    • setup_needed: For one action run on its own, a no-argument callable that returns why the setup must run first, or None (a check that raises counts as a reason). With a reason, ensure_category_setup() prints it in one line and runs the setup. api returns one when the lane's test database is missing, unreadable or lacks one of its fixture users.
    • default_isolation: The isolation class of every unit that declares neither isolation nor exclusive_because — see Declaring a class — and earning it.
  • A set of actions (e.g., "decimal-precision", "all"), where each action points to:
    • func: The Python callable that starts the test.
    • name: A human-readable title.
    • desc: A short description of the test action.
    • prereq / tests / note: Optional flags and metadata for dependencies.
    • in_all: True unless the action is registered in_all=False or named_only=True. False leaves it out of its category's serial all: an action whose files another action already runs, such as an aggregate alias, or the four per-spec actions of front-ai-export that cutover runs in one invocation. Such an action is still a claimant in the frontend consolidated pass: it gets its verdict from the run that covers its files.
    • named_only: Present, and True, only for an action registered named_only=True: it runs only when named on the command line, on any lane. It implies in_all=False, and group_frontend_units() (_consolidate.py) leaves it out of the frontend consolidated pass too, whatever it launches. It exists for an action that needs a lane of its own while other actions already run its files: today front-utility cloud-smoke, refused unless the lane is managed. On a managed lane its profile check passes while the inventory collects launches, so with in_all=False alone it would have stayed in front-utility all, and all-frontend would have run seven specs twice. The backend's consolidated and parallel passes do not read it: no backend action needs it today.

docs.title: 📊 Coverage Isolation & Swap Pipeline (_coverage.py)
docs.text:
Because backend and frontend tests run in different modes (some as direct test scripts, others as separate server subprocesses driven by Playwright E2E tests), they write coverage reports using parallel = true.

By default, running coverage combine would merge and delete all coverage databases. To prevent backend and frontend reports from colliding, the test runner implements a swap-in/swap-out pipeline:

---
config:
  layout: elk
---
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant Data as .coverage_data/
    participant Root as Root Dir (.coverage)
    participant Pytest as Pytest Runner
    participant Reporter as _coverage.py

    Note over Data, Root: Before running pytest
    Data->>Root: Restore backend database (copy .coverage_data/backend ➔ .coverage)

    Note over Root, Pytest: During execution
    Pytest->>Root: pytest-cov runs and appends new coverage data to .coverage

    Note over Root, Data: After execution (finally block)
    Root->>Data: Backup accumulated database (copy .coverage ➔ .coverage_data/backend)

    Note over Data, Reporter: finalization (_finalize_coverage)
    Reporter->>Data: Read .coverage_data/backend ➔ generate htmlcov-backend/
    Reporter->>Data: Read .coverage_data/frontend ➔ generate htmlcov-backend-e2e/
    Reporter->>Data: Merge both databases ➔ generate combined htmlcov/

JS/Svelte coverage follows a parallel, independent path

_finalize_js_coverage() merges monocart's raw output instead of coverage.py databases, producing the reports under frontend/coverage-js/. The two pipelines never share state — see Coverage Model.

docs.title: Coverage File Invariants
docs.text:
• .coverage: Active working copy. Stored in the root folder, updated during pytest runs, and combined dynamically.
  • .coverage_data/backend: Accumulated backend test coverage. Persisted here between backend test runs.
  • .coverage_data/frontend: Subprocess coverage captured from the backend server while running Playwright E2E tests.
  • .coverage_data/parts/: Parallel-pass output. The JUnit reports (junit.wN.xml) stay at its top level; worker coverage data files live in a directory per runner process, run-<YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS>-<pid>/, named .coverage.p<pass>.wN, where the pass number counts that run's parallel passes. Spawn children and multiprocessing's resource tracker write .coverage.p<pass>.wN.<host>.pid<N>.X<random>x beside them (coverage.py renames each to ….X<random>x.H<hash>h when it finishes writing), and can finish after the workers return. That is why coverage combine is given the directory, never a list of names: a name listed before such a rename made the whole combine fail. A part that lands after coverage's own listing is folded in by a later round (three rounds at most). A part holding data is removed only once it has been folded into the accumulated database. After a successful combine the run directory is removed; when a combine fails, the directory stays, the error names it together with the parts left in it, and the parallel pass is reported red. A finished part (coverage's final ….H<hash>h name) that holds no data is removed and named in a warning, and does not fail the combine: it is the schema without a row, left when a SIGTERM stopped its writer while coverage.py was already saving, so its data never reached the file; a part with a transient name is never judged empty, since it may still be filling up. --cov-clean-backend empties parts/ of coverage data — loose .coverage* files left by older runs and run-* directories — and keeps the JUnit reports.
  • .coverage_data/unit_durations.json: Measured seconds per test unit, read by the scheduler to balance the next run.

Why per-worker files rather than one shared database

Python coverage is a SQLite database and combining is native to it, which is exactly what makes per-worker files viable. The copy-in/copy-out of a single global .coverage in run_command is the point at which the old design forced serialisation: a global mutable file cannot be shared by two processes. JS coverage cannot follow suit — its raw V8 data is a set of byte offsets into one specific bundle, so it cannot survive a rebuild and is wiped unconditionally by design.

docs.title: 📂 Submodule Directory Map
docs.text: File Purpose scripts/test_runner/__init__.py Package initialiser: puts the project root first on sys.path, makes it the working directory, and re-exports main, register_subparser (which dev.py uses to add ./dev.py test), _ensure_test_users and TEST_REGISTRY. scripts/test_runner/__main__.py Lets the package run as python -m scripts.test_runner [category] [action]: calls main() and exits with code 130 on Ctrl-C. scripts/test_runner/_cli.py Defines the argparse command hierarchy (e.g., ./dev.py test [category] [action]), listings (--list), and executes the matched callback. scripts/test_runner/_registry.py Imports and invokes the registry population hook of every category module to assemble TEST_REGISTRY. scripts/test_runner/_suites.py Contains logic to run entire groups of tests (all, all-backend, all-frontend) and clean up coverage folders. scripts/test_runner/_run_cache.py The run cache behind --resume, --fresh-run and --run-status (.run_cache.json: per suite, the tests passed and the last failure), and the campaign timing printed at the end of a run (.campaign.json). Both files sit next to the module and are gitignored. scripts/test_runner/_coverage.py Implements database merging, report generation (htmlcov-backend/, htmlcov-backend-e2e/, htmlcov/), the JS/Svelte pipeline (frontend/coverage-js/), and coverage show, which opens a report's index.html in the browser. scripts/test_runner/_inventory.py Derives the test units from the registry without executing them, classifies each one by isolation class, and answers the reachability questions used by check-orphans. scripts/test_runner/_scheduler.py Turns inventory plus --workers N into an execution plan, balancing groups longest-processing-time first from persisted per-unit durations. scripts/test_runner/_executor.py Runs the plan's groups as concurrent processes, hands each worker its exclusive resource lot, and combines the per-worker coverage databases afterwards. scripts/test_runner/_server.py One test backend for the whole run (SharedTestServer), opened by _cli.py when the invocation needs a server (api, e2e, the all* suites, frontend runs with Playwright specs): dev.py server --test --no-reload --no-scheduler, plus --coverage under Python coverage, in its own process group, with its uvicorn workers sized to the client workers. start() refuses a port that another process holds, then builds before it spawns: build_server_prerequisites() runs dev.py server --test --build-only in the foreground, its output on the terminal, with the runner's environment but not the coverage wiring the server gets (the tooling is not measured). That rebuilds the frontend (debug) and the MkDocs site when they are missing or stale and refreshes the JS cache; a failed build starts no server. The backend spawned next finds those builds up to date, so STARTUP_TIMEOUT (300 s; LIBREFOLIO_TEST_STARTUP_TIMEOUT overrides it, in whole seconds) measures its start alone. Before this step the server made the builds inside that wait, about 130 s after a large merge, unseen: its output was discarded at the time. Its stdout and stderr (dev.py, uvicorn, the app's console log) go to one file for the whole run, not only the startup: shared-backend.log, in the run's log directory (--log-dir, .testLog by default), next to the per-unit logs. The file is emptied when the run's backend first starts and appended to when the backend restarts mid-run around db create, so it keeps every start's output; the next run archives it with the per-unit logs (prepare_log_dir, 00_archive/). A file and not a pipe, so a server that writes a lot never blocks; when the output goes there, the spawn sets PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 for the whole exec chain, so dev.py's own lines come out in order among uvicorn's. When a start fails (the process exits during startup, or STARTUP_TIMEOUT passes), the runner prints, under its error line, the file's path and the last 30 lines written by that start, never an earlier start's, or (no output) when that start wrote nothing; it reads at most the file's last 64 KiB. With --log-dir "" there is no file and the output is discarded. It sets LIBREFOLIO_TEST_SHARED_SERVER=1 so that pytest modules and Playwright attach to it instead of starting their own, and stops with SIGTERM and a grace period: 30 s under coverage, 10 s otherwise, the server's own shutdown budget (LIBREFOLIO_SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT_SECONDS, 8 s by default) plus a margin, so that outside coverage a Shared backend ignored SIGTERM warning means the server broke that budget. It steps aside while db create rebuilds the database file (database_file_owned_exclusively()). --no-shared-server turns it off. scripts/test_runner/_consolidate.py Groups a frontend category's units into one vitest invocation and one Playwright invocation per project selection (desktop only, or desktop and mobile; in batches of 8 specs under JS coverage), then reads the JSON reporters back into a per-spec verdict. scripts/test_runner/_consolidate_backend.py The backend counterpart: when a whole category or suite runs, one pytest invocation per category instead of one per unit — services, utils, schemas, api, e2e, in that order, while db and external keep one per action — with the JUnit report read back into a per-file verdict, so the summary and --resume stay per unit. scripts/test_runner/_common.py Shared helpers and run-wide state: run_command (launches one unit; for pytest it adds the coverage flags, swaps the accumulated coverage database in and out, and points the child at the test database), _run_test_suite (the serial loop of a suite, with the run-cache bookkeeping), tee_output (behind --log-file and the per-unit logs), and the registry helpers make_category, add_test, run_category_setup (runs a category's declared setup, once per invocation) and ensure_category_setup (before one action run on its own, runs that setup when the category's setup_needed gives a reason). scripts/test_runner/_archive.py Archives test artefacts — the previous --log-dir logs, coverage databases before they are replaced or cleaned, the test-DB snapshot taken at the end of a run with a log directory — as <target>/00_archive/<label>_<YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS>.tar.xz, compressed with the standard library only (falling back to .tar.bz2, .tar.gz, then plain .tar when the interpreter lacks lzma). It also names the per-unit logs, <category>__<unit>.log. scripts/test_runner/_backend_*.py One module per backend category; _backend_api.py registers both api and e2e. The actions launch pytest, except db create and db populate, which build and fill the test database. scripts/test_runner/_frontend_*.py One module per frontend category (utility, broker, user, fx, asset, transaction, portfolio, ai_export): its Playwright specs and Vitest files. _frontend_common.py matches the pattern but is not a category — see the next row. scripts/test_runner/_frontend_common.py Shared frontend helpers: the frontend build check, the test-DB population and E2E user creation (each done once per setup scope), the Playwright launcher, and the --list output of every category.

docs.title: 🛠️ Developer Guide: Adding a Test Action
docs.text:
To add a new test action to an existing category:

  1. Open the category module (e.g., _backend_utils.py for utility tests).
  2. Write a function that executes your test suite using the shared runner helpers. Accept test_names: an action registered with the default test_names=True receives the test names the user passes, and ./dev.py test <category> --help marks it [TEST_NAME]. One registered with test_names=False refuses them: the runner exits with code 2 before anything runs, rather than running the whole action as if no name had been given. run_command requires a description, the label it prints, also used to name the unit's log file: 
    def utils_my_new_utility(verbose: bool = False, test_names: list = None) -> bool:
    """Run tests for the new utility helper."""
    print_section("Utils: My New Utility")
    # pipenv run python -m pytest <path> -v (no "pipenv run" in Docker), plus -k "<a> or <b>" for the names given
    cmd = _build_pytest_cmd("backend/test_scripts/test_utilities/test_my_new_utility.py", test_names)
    # True when the command exits with code 0
    return run_command(cmd, "My new utility tests", verbose=verbose)
  3. Locate the populate_registry function at the bottom of the file and register your action: 
    add_test(cat, "my-new-utility", utils_my_new_utility, name="My New Utility", desc="Tests my new utility module")
  4. Once registered, it is automatically exposed in the CLI: 
    ./dev.py test utils my-new-utility
  5. Nothing else is needed. The category's all list is derived from the registry by _get_category_tests_for_all(), so a registered action is reachable by construction — the state "registered but never executed" is no longer expressible. Pass in_all=False only when another action already runs the same files, as with an aggregate alias. Pass named_only=True for an action that must run only when named, on any lane: one that needs a lane of its own while other actions already run its files, as front-utility cloud-smoke on a managed lane. It implies in_all=False, and the frontend consolidated pass leaves it out too (see Registry Entry Shape).

Never hand-write an all list

_get_category_tests_for_all() does two jobs, and the second one is easy to forget: it derives the list and it drops the actions the parallel pass has already covered (_SKIP_ACTIONS). An all that builds its own list therefore does not diverge in some distant future — it re-runs, in the serial pass, everything the workers just ran.

external_all() was the last such list on the backend, and it made test_fx_providers.py run twice under --workers 4. Nothing turned red; the only symptom was a test count 28 higher than the serial run's. Derive the list, always.

Verify with the orphan check

./dev.py test check-orphans

This reports both test files that no action mentions and actions that no all reaches, reasoning about launched paths rather than about strings in the source.

docs.title: 🧩 Gate and Runner Units
docs.text:
The units below test the project's own tooling rather than application helpers. All are PURE: no database, no server, no network.

Sub-command What It Tests gate-i18n-usage The three-verdict i18n key classifier in scripts/i18n_usage.py, which ./dev.py i18n audit uses to report unused keys: used (proven), dead (proven absent), or not verified (the key's family exists but its last segment is produced at runtime). It checks typed-union expansion, constant namespaces, both branches of a ternary or of a conditional prefix, backend literals as the vocabulary of dynamic segments, and that test sources never count as evidence. Each case asserts what must be condemned and what must survive (backend/test_scripts/test_utilities/test_i18n_usage_gate.py). gate-i18n-catalog The translation catalogue that scripts/i18n_catalog.py builds from its sources — frontend/src/lib/i18n/base/, one folder per subsystem with its prefixes.txt, each plugin's i18n/ fragment — with every rule proven both ways on synthetic trees: a key belongs to the plugin that holds it, else to the subsystem with the longest declared prefix, else to base; a key in two sources, a string in one source against a branch in another, or a key outside the folder its prefix names is an error; a missing translation is filled from English with a warning when building and is an error under the strict check; the build writes only what changed, read-only, with a sha256 stamp, and refuses a hand-edited file; add routing, move, split, check --against and the three-way absorb. On the repository: the sources merge strictly in the four languages, and git ignores the generated files and none of the sources (Internationalization; backend/test_scripts/test_utilities/test_i18n_catalog_gate.py). gate-plugin-layout Every first-party plugin of the six families (brim_providers, asset_source_providers, fx_providers, risk_plugins, signal_plugins, tool_plugins) is a folder <family>/<name>/ holding plugin.py and an __init__.py that is its docstring and nothing else, and no family keeps a plugin as a single module. Over backend/app, backend/test_scripts, scripts and dev.py, no import or string (a patch() target, a logger name, a __module__) reaches a plugin's package instead of its plugin module or a _* helper beside it. The sources are parsed with ast, never imported (Plugin Folder Layout; backend/test_scripts/test_utilities/test_plugin_layout_gate.py). gate-plugin-i18n-ownership Each plugin's translations live in its own i18n/ fragment, judged by the metadata its registry publishes. A plugin's space is brimPlugins.<code> (the code being its folder's name); assets.providerParams.<provider_code> and pluginSettings.asset.<provider_code> for an asset plugin; pluginSettings.fx.<code> for an FX plugin, the code as the registry has it (pluginSettings.fx.ECB); the parent of a signal's display_name_key or of a risk analytic's name_i18n_key; or exactly a Tool's name_i18n_key and description_i18n_key. R1: every fragment key lies in its plugin's space. R2: every key a plugin declares in its exclusive space lives in its fragment, the keys of an asset or FX plugin's settings_fields included (each field's label_key and description_key, each option's label_key). R3: no fragment key lies in another plugin's space or is declared by another plugin. R4: every catalogue key under an exclusive space lives in that plugin's fragment, Tools aside. Each rule is proven both ways on synthetic trees, and a sentinel fails on a published key field the gate does not read, in the plugins' settings and in the attributes of PluginSettingField and SettingOption too (The Ownership Gate; backend/test_scripts/test_utilities/test_plugin_i18n_ownership_gate.py). gate-event-loop-io No async def under backend/app/api/v1/ directly calls a synchronous function of the BRIM file store, backend/app/services/brim/brim_provider.py (its top-level defs and their module-level aliases, such as broker_metadata_lock = _broker_metadata_lock): that I/O would run on the event loop, so it goes through await asyncio.to_thread(fn, ...). Every way an API file binds the module or imports one of its functions by name is followed (from-import, import … as, plain, relative, lazy). A reference handed to to_thread, the body of a nested def or lambda, an awaited coroutine of the module and a synchronous handler are not flagged. Control cases prove on in-memory sources that the detector sees a direct call and leaves the allowed shapes alone, and the scan must reach an API file that imports the store: an empty scan would pass without checking anything. The sources are parsed with ast, never imported (Event Loop Blocking Rule; backend/test_scripts/test_utilities/test_event_loop_brim_io_gate.py). runtime-isolation The runtime lane contract: test-port and data-directory resolution with its production guards, propagation of the lane to child processes and nested Pipenv runs, the lane-identity readiness probe, and ownership of the shared test server, which never reuses or signals a process it did not start (backend/test_scripts/test_utilities/test_runtime_isolation.py).

List every unit of the category, each with its description, with ./dev.py test utils --help. ./dev.py test utils <unit> --list lists the tests of one unit without running them, and ./dev.py test utils all --list those of the whole category (see Running Tests).

docs.title: 📅 Day Count Conventions
docs.text:
A Day Count Convention determines how interest accrues over time for a variety of financial instruments, such as bonds, loans, and mortgages. It defines two things:

  1. How to calculate the number of days between two dates.
  2. How to calculate the number of days in a year.

docs.title: 🔧 Usage in LibreFolio
docs.text:
Day count conventions are actively used by the Scheduled Investment asset source provider for synthetic yield calculations. The function calculate_day_count_fraction() lives in the financial-math home (backend/app/services/financial_math/interest.py), implements all four conventions, and returns a Decimal time fraction on which the Scheduled Investment provider builds its interest accrual.

The default convention is ACT/365.

docs.title: 📅 ACT/365 (Actual/365)
docs.text:
• Days: The actual number of days between two dates.
  • Year: Assumed to be 365 days.
  • Formula: \(t = \frac{\text{actual days}}{365}\)
  • Usage: Common in UK money markets and for some government bonds. Default in LibreFolio.

docs.title: 📅 ACT/360 (Actual/360)
docs.text:
• Days: The actual number of days between two dates.
  • Year: Assumed to be 360 days.
  • Formula: \(t = \frac{\text{actual days}}{360}\)
  • Usage: Very common in US money markets and for commercial loans.

docs.title: 📐 30/360 (Bond Basis)
docs.text:
• Days: Calculated assuming every month has 30 days.
  • Year: Assumed to be 360 days.
  • Formula: \(t = \frac{360(Y_2 - Y_1) + 30(M_2 - M_1) + (D_2 - D_1)}{360}\)
  • Usage: Standard for US corporate bonds and many municipal bonds.

docs.title: 📅 ACT/ACT (Actual/Actual)
docs.text:
• Days: The actual number of days between two dates.
  • Year: The actual number of days in the year (365 or 366 for leap years).
  • Formula: \(t = \frac{\text{actual days}}{365 \text{ or } 366}\)
  • Usage: Standard for US Treasury bonds. Handles leap years correctly by calculating the fraction for each year separately.

Why does this matter?

The difference between conventions can be significant for large principals or long durations. For example, 30 days on a €1M loan at 5%: ACT/365 gives €4,109.59 in interest, while ACT/360 gives €4,166.67 — a €57 difference from the same 30-day period.

Day Count Convention on Wikipedia
