docs.title: 📈 Performance Metrics
docs.text: When evaluating the success of an investment portfolio, looking only at the total balance or absolute profit is not enough. To truly understand performance, you need standardized metrics that answer different questions: "How did my assets perform?", "How good was my timing?", and "What is the return on this specific trade?".

docs.title: 🎭 The Two Actors in Your Portfolio
docs.text:
To understand why multiple metrics exist, imagine there are two different "actors" managing your wealth:

  1. The Market (The Assets): Causes the prices of the things you own to go up or down.
  2. You (The Investor): Decides when to deposit or withdraw cash from the portfolio.

These two actors can have vastly different performances. You might pick an excellent stock (The Market performs well), but you might buy it at the very top just before a crash (You perform poorly). LibreFolio uses different metrics to isolate these two behaviors.

docs.title: 📚 Topics in this Chapter
docs.text: LibreFolio's performance metrics are organized around three calculation engines. Each has its own overview page with the full mathematical model.

docs.title: ⚙️ Portfolio Engine
docs.text:
Aggregate, WAC-based accounting for the whole portfolio (or any broker/asset scope).

Metric / Concept Description Portfolio Engine Overview Complete mathematical model: unified price resolver, WAC, aggregation, 3-pool model, contribution, one daily replay. Price Resolution Unified resolver tiers: MARKET → TRADE_AVG → CARRIED → MISSING, with native marks and per-date FX. Net Asset Value (NAV) Total market valuation of the portfolio (assets + cash + in-transit), using the unified resolver. Book Value Historical accounting cost of open positions (WAC × qty) plus cash. Difference from NAV = unrealized P&L. Period P&L Cash-flow adjusted monetary profit/loss in a window. Decomposes into: unrealized delta + realized + income − fees. Includes per-asset contribution attribution. Deposited Capital & Total P&L Net external capital since inception. Documents the 3-pool event-driven cash decomposition model (K, R, W) with formal transaction-level update rules. Timing Effect Difference between Cumulative MWRR and Cumulative TWRR — quantifies the impact of cash flow timing on returns. Simple ROI Percentage return relative to net invested capital. Simple but subject to cash flow dilution. Net Annualized Return Net CAGR definitions for holdings, period contribution, and FIFO lots, with 30-day minimum window. Yield on Cost Trailing-365-day gross dividend/interest, each amount with its sign, per eligible historical unit, divided by average purchase price (WAC) for each asset/broker pair. TWRR Time-Weighted Rate of Return. Pure asset/strategy performance, neutralizing deposit/withdrawal timing. MWRR (XIRR) Money-Weighted Rate of Return. Personal investor performance accounting for cash flow timing. Annualized and Cumulative forms.

docs.title: 🔬 FIFO Engine
docs.text:
Per-lot accounting: tracks each acquisition batch through its own lifecycle instead of blending it into one average.

Metric / Concept Description FIFO Engine Overview Lot lifecycle states, chronological event processing, FIFO matching, splits, and transfers between brokers. FIFO Lot Analysis Per-lot complement to WAC: tracks each acquisition batch through its own lifecycle, matches sells in FIFO order, and computes open/total return per lot.

docs.title: 📊 Weighted Average Cost
docs.text: Metric / Concept Description Weighted Average Cost Inventory-aware iterative WAC per position (broker, asset), each acquisition at its own date's exchange rate. Computed once per report, then replayed by the engine's daily loop.

docs.title: ⚖️ Metric Comparison Guide
docs.text: To help you choose the right metric for your analysis, use this comparison guide:

docs.title: 💼 1. Net Asset Value (NAV) / Net Worth
docs.text:
• Core Question: "How much is the portfolio in the selected scope worth right now?"
  • Formula Concept: \(\text{Market Value} + \text{Cash} + \text{In Transit Assets}\) at end of period.
  • Best Use Case: Snapshot of absolute wealth on the selected end date (date_to).

docs.title: 📖 2. Book Value
docs.text:
• Core Question: "How much did my current portfolio cost to build?"
  • Formula Concept: \(\text{Open Cost Basis} + \text{Cash} + \text{In Transit Book Value}\) using Weighted Average Cost (WAC).
  • Best Use Case: Evaluating acquisition costs and comparing with current market value (NAV) to find latent gains.

docs.title: 📊 3. Period P&L
docs.text:
• Core Question: "How much money did I actually earn or lose during this period?"
  • Formula Concept: \(\text{NAV}_{\text{end}} - \text{NAV}_{\text{start}} - \Delta\text{CapitalBaseline}\).
  • Best Use Case: Measuring period gains in absolute currency, independent of investor cash injections/withdrawals.

docs.title: ⏱️ 4. Timing Effect
docs.text:
• Core Question: "How did the timing and size of my cash flows affect my overall return compared to a buy-and-hold strategy?"
  • Formula Concept: \(\text{MWRR}_{\text{cumulative}} - \text{TWRR}_{\text{cumulative}}\).
  • Best Use Case: Diagnosing whether deposits and withdrawals added value (\(>0\) pp) or dragged down performance (\(<0\) pp).

docs.title: 📉 5. Simple ROI
docs.text:
• Core Question: "How much did I gain relative to the net capital I invested?"
  • Formula Denominator: Capital baseline, including priced in-kind capital.
  • Limitations: Does not account for when cash flows occurred, leading to cash flow dilution when subsequently buying more of an asset.

docs.title: ⏱️ 6. TWRR (Time-Weighted Rate of Return)
docs.text:
• Core Question: "How did my chosen asset allocation/strategy perform, ignoring my cash timing?"
  • Formula Concept: Breaks the timeline at each cash flow, calculates sub-period returns, and multiplies them.
  • Best Use Case: Comparing your performance with external benchmarks (like the S&P 500) or evaluating the pure performance of the assets.

docs.title: 📈 7. Annualized MWRR (Money-Weighted Rate of Return)
docs.text:
• Core Question: "At what compound annual rate did my actual capital grow, considering my deposits and withdrawals?"
  • Formula Concept: Solves for the internal rate of return (\(r\)) that brings the net present value of all cash flows to zero.
  • Best Use Case: Comparing your personal performance against long-term interest rates or evaluating compound growth over long horizons. Can be highly volatile on short windows.

docs.title: 📊 8. Cumulative MWRR
docs.text:
• Core Question: "What is the equivalent money-weighted cumulative return over this selected time window?"
  • Formula Concept: Compounds the annualized MWRR for the actual number of days elapsed.
  • Best Use Case: Serial charts and dashboard widgets to compare visual performance trends side-by-side with TWRR and ROI.

docs.title: 💸 9. Yield on Cost
docs.text:
• Core Question: "How much gross dividend and interest income did each current unit produce over the last 365 calendar dates relative to its average purchase price?"
  • Formula Concept: Sums signed, transaction-date-FX income per eligible prior-day long unit, adjusts for linked splits, then divides by average purchase price (WAC) at the report end date.
  • Best Use Case: Comparing the recorded income productivity of open asset/broker positions without confusing it with market dividend yield, CAGR, or bond YTM.

docs.title: 💡 The Practical Example (TWRR vs MWRR vs ROI)
docs.text:
Let's look at an extreme example to see how TWRR, MWRR, and Simple ROI tell different, but mathematically correct, stories.

  • Month 1: You buy €1,000 of a stock. The next month, the stock doubles (+100%). You now have €2,000.
  • Month 2: You deposit another €100,000 into the exact same stock. You now have €102,000 invested.
  • Month 3: The stock drops by -10%. Your total capital drops to €91,800.

Here is what LibreFolio will calculate for this scenario:

docs.title: 📊 Cumulative TWRR: +80.00%
docs.text:
The assets you picked went up +100%, and then dropped -10%. Mathematically:

\[ (1 + 1.00) \times (1 - 0.10) - 1 = +80.00\% \]

This isolates the pure performance of the stock. Your asset picking was excellent. If you had invested all your money on day 1, you would have made an 80% return.

docs.title: 📉 Simple ROI: -9.11%
docs.text:
You deposited a total of €101,000 out of your own pocket (€1,000 + €100,000), but you currently hold €91,800:

\[ ROI = \frac{91,800 - 101,000}{101,000} = -9.11\% \]

This represents your actual, raw wallet gain/loss relative to your net invested capital.

docs.title: 💵 Cumulative MWRR: -16.99%
docs.text:
Because you deposited €100,000 right at the peak before a drop, your timing dragged down your return significantly:

\[ \text{MWRR}_{\text{cumulative}} \approx -16.99\% \]

This money-weighted cumulative return represents the performance of a "theoretical euro" under your actual cash flow timing.

docs.title: 📈 Annualized MWRR: -67.19%
docs.text:
Since the substantial drop occurred over a very short time window (31 days) on a massive capital base (€100,000), the annualized compound rate of loss is very high:

\[ \text{MWRR}_{\text{annualized}} \approx -67.19\% \]

This represents the annualized speed of capital loss over this specific window.

docs.title: ⚖️ Why LibreFolio shows both side-by-side
docs.text:
By placing TWRR and MWRR next to each other on your Dashboard, LibreFolio gives you an immediate behavioral diagnosis:

  • TWRR > MWRR: "You are picking good investments, but your timing is bad. You are likely buying at the top (FOMO) and dragging your personal returns down."
  • MWRR > TWRR: "You have excellent timing! You are buying assets at a discount when the market drops, boosting your personal returns above the market average."

docs.title: 🔗 UI Integration & Dashboard Help Links
docs.text:
To aid navigation, the three KPI cards on the LibreFolio dashboard — Period P&L, Returns, and Net Worth — each carry a help icon. The path to these theory chapters is two steps:

  1. The help icon opens the matching section of the user guide's KPI Cards page (Card 1, Card 2, Card 3).
  2. From there, each metric links to its financial theory chapter: Period P&L, Book Value, ROI, TWRR, MWRR, Timing Effect, NAV / Net Worth, Deposited Capital & Total P&L.

Elsewhere in the app, the WAC preview in the transaction form links directly to the Weighted Average Cost chapter, the Holdings table links its YOC column to Yield on Cost, and each chart signal/indicator links to its own theory page.

docs.title: 💡 What is WAC?
docs.text:
The Weighted Average Cost (WAC) is the average unit cost of an asset in a portfolio, weighted by the quantity acquired at each price.

It answers the question: "On average, how much did I pay per unit for this asset?"

Other names

  • PMC — Prezzo Medio di Carico (Italy)
  • ACB — Average Cost Basis (Canada, US)
  • CMP — Coût Moyen Pondéré (France)

docs.title: 🧮 Formula
docs.text:
The WAC is computed iteratively as each transaction is processed chronologically:

\[ WAC_{new} = \frac{WAC_{current} \times Q_{pool} + Cost_{unit} \times Q_{tx}}{Q_{pool} + Q_{tx}} \]

Where:

  • \(WAC_{current}\) = current weighted average cost before this transaction
  • \(Q_{pool}\) = total quantity held in the pool before this transaction
  • \(Cost_{unit}\) = per-unit acquisition cost of the new transaction — what was actually paid, in the currency the WAC is kept in, converted at the rate of the transaction's own date (see Multi-Currency Handling)
  • \(Q_{tx}\) = quantity added by the new transaction

Equivalently, LibreFolio keeps the pool's total cost \(C_{pool}\) next to its quantity, with \(WAC = C_{pool} / Q_{pool}\): an acquisition adds its cost, a reduction of \(q\) units removes \(C_{pool} \cdot q / Q_{pool}\).

docs.title: ⚙️ How LibreFolio Computes WAC
docs.text: LibreFolio uses an inventory-aware iterative algorithm that processes all qualifying transactions for a given (broker, asset) pair in chronological order. The same algorithm serves every screen that shows an average cost: the Dashboard, the Positions table, the lots analysis and the transaction preview.

docs.title: 🏷️ Transaction Effects
docs.text:
Each transaction contributes to the WAC computation in one of these ways:

Effect Condition Impact on WAC Weighted qty > 0 with a known cost above zero WAC moves toward the new acquisition cost Quantity reduced qty < 0 Exits at current WAC — WAC unchanged, pool shrinks Dilution qty > 0 at zero cost Pool grows, numerator unchanged → WAC decreases Split Adjustment linked to a split event Quantity rescaled, total cost unchanged → WAC divided by the split ratio Unknown cost qty > 0 with no known cost: a transfer or adjustment without cost basis override Pool grows without cost — the WAC is incomplete (see Cost Basis Override)

docs.title: 📅 Same-Day Ordering
docs.text:
When multiple transactions occur on the same date:

  1. Additions first (qty > 0) — processed before reductions
  2. Reductions second (qty < 0) — ensures the pool doesn't go transiently negative

docs.title: 🔻 Pool Depletion
docs.text:
• When the quantity reaches 0, the last reduction takes the whole remaining cost, so total cost is conserved exactly; the pool restarts from zero, and a later purchase opens a new, complete pool
  • A reduction larger than the pool is clamped to the quantity available

docs.title: 📝 Practical Examples
docs.text:
Example 1: Two Buys — WAC rises Date Type Qty Unit Cost Pool Qty WAC Apr 1 BUY 10 $150 10 $150.00 Apr 15 BUY 5 $180 15 $160.00 \[ WAC = \frac{150 \times 10 + 180 \times 5}{10 + 5} = \frac{2400}{15} = 160.00 \]

The second buy at a higher price pulls the WAC up.

Example 2: Buy then Sell — WAC unchanged Date Type Qty Unit Cost Pool Qty WAC Apr 1 BUY 10 $150 10 $150.00 Apr 15 SELL -5 (at WAC) 5 $150.00

The SELL removes units at the current WAC ($150). The WAC stays unchanged — only the pool shrinks.

Example 3: Zero-Cost Acquisition — Dilution Date Type Qty Unit Cost Pool Qty WAC Apr 1 BUY 10 $150 10 $150.00 May 1 ADJUSTMENT +5 $0 15 $100.00 \[ WAC = \frac{150 \times 10 + 0 \times 5}{10 + 5} = \frac{1500}{15} = 100.00 \]

The WAC is diluted because 5 units entered at zero cost — an adjustment whose cost basis override is zero, such as an airdrop. A 3-for-2 split linked to its split event reaches the same $100.00 without any acquisition: the pool keeps its $1,500 and spreads it over 15 units.

docs.title: 🔄 Cost Basis Override
docs.text:
For transfers and adjustments, LibreFolio supports a cost basis override: a unit cost, in a currency of your choice, that represents the historical cost of the units coming in. A transfer or adjustment that adds quantity needs one: the transaction form requires it.

When set (manual mode):

  • The transaction enters the WAC computation as a normal weighted acquisition costing \(\text{override} \times Q_{tx}\), converted at the transaction date like any purchase
  • This preserves cost continuity across brokers (e.g., when transferring from broker A to broker B)
  • An override of zero is a free acquisition: the dilution of Example 3

When missing:

  • The cost of those units is unknown, not zero: they enter the pool without any cost, and the WAC stays incomplete until the position is closed
  • The Dashboard shows that position's average cost and unrealized P&L as unavailable and warns about the missing cost basis; the transaction preview counts the units at zero (dilution)

When auto mode (cost_basis_mode = "auto"):

  • LibreFolio computes the WAC of the source position — for a transfer, the sending broker's position when the units left (the transfer-out date), before the outgoing leg; for an adjustment, the position itself at the transaction date, without this transaction — and stores it as the override
  • From then on the transaction is an ordinary weighted acquisition at that unit cost. For an adjustment on the same position, the WAC therefore stays algebraically unchanged, in the currency it was computed in:
\[ WAC_{new} = \frac{WAC \times Q_{pool} + WAC \times Q_{tx}}{Q_{pool} + Q_{tx}} = WAC \]

Auto mode in the UI

In the transaction form, the Auto toggle computes the value when you validate: the preview shows the suggested WAC and the transactions it comes from, each with its effect.

Example 4: Transfer in Auto Mode — the cost follows the units

Broker A holds the pool of Example 1 and sends 3 units to broker B, which held none:

Broker Date Type Qty Unit Cost Pool Qty WAC A Apr 1 BUY 10 $150 10 $150.00 A Apr 15 BUY 5 $180 15 $160.00 A May 1 TRANSFER out −3 (at WAC) 12 $160.00 B May 1 TRANSFER in (auto) +3 $160 (A's WAC) 3 $160.00

In auto mode the receiving side takes the sender's WAC as its cost basis override: broker B starts at broker A's average, and the $480 of cost moves with the 3 units.

docs.title: 🌍 Multi-Currency Handling
docs.text:
The WAC is kept in a single currency, the target currency \(T\), and every acquisition enters it at its historical cost: the amount actually paid, converted at the rate of the acquisition's own date \(d_i\):

\[ c_i^{T} = P_i \cdot \mathrm{fx}\bigl(\mathrm{ccy}(P_i),\, T,\, d_i\bigr), \qquad \mathrm{fx}(T, T, d) = 1 \]

Here \(P_i\) is the cash paid for a BUY, in its cash currency, or \(\text{override} \times Q_{tx}\) in the override's currency for a transfer or adjustment. An amount already in \(T\) needs no rate at all; otherwise, when the exact date has no rate, the latest rate before it is used.

The cost basis of a position is then

\[ \mathrm{CB}(a,b,t) = q(a,b,t) \times \mathrm{WAC}^{T}(a,b,t) \]

with no exchange rate at \(t\): it is what was paid, and it does not move when exchange rates move. For an asset priced in another currency, the exchange-rate effect therefore sits in the unrealized gain/loss — market value at the day's rate minus historical cost — where the Dashboard splits it out (see Period P&L).

The target currency depends on where the WAC is shown:

Where Target currency \(T\) Dashboard, Positions table, realized sales, Yield on Cost The display (report) currency Lots analysis WAC lines The currency of the analysis Transaction preview, automatic cost basis The currency picked in the preview, otherwise the currency of the latest acquisition PAC planner The planner's currency

The latest acquisition's currency is the currency paid by the most recent transaction that added quantity — a deterministic rule; on a tie, the first one recorded wins. A split, or an acquisition of unknown cost, falls back to the asset's own currency.

Example 5: A dollar asset bought with euro, display currency EUR Date Type Qty Paid Rate USD→EUR Cost in EUR Apr 1 BUY 10 €400 — (paid in EUR) €400.00 May 1 BUY 5 300 USD 0.90 €270.00 \[ WAC^{EUR} = \frac{400 + 270}{10 + 5} = \frac{670}{15} \approx 44.67 \text{ EUR} \]

The first purchase needs no rate: its cost is exactly the €400 paid. The position's cost basis stays €670 whatever the dollar does afterwards; a weaker dollar lowers the market value in euro and shows up as an unrealized loss.

FX Rate Availability

When no rate exists on or before an acquisition date, LibreFolio never counts that cost as zero. The units enter the pool without their cost and the WAC is marked incomplete: the transaction preview shows no WAC and lists the missing pair with its dates, the Dashboard shows the position's average cost and unrealized P&L as unavailable, and the lots analysis leaves those days out of its WAC lines. The UI warns about the missing FX pairs and provides quick-actions to add or sync them.

docs.title: 🎯 Where WAC is Used in LibreFolio
docs.text:
• Cost basis: \(\text{CB}(a,b,t) = q(a,b,t) \times \text{WAC}^{T}(a,b,t)\), historical, with no conversion at \(t\)
  • Realized P&L on SELL: \(\text{realized} = P_{\text{sell}} - q_{\text{sold}} \times \text{WAC}^{T}_{\text{pre-sell}}\), with the proceeds \(P_{\text{sell}}\) converted at the sale date and the units sold leaving at their historical cost. An outgoing adjustment realizes the same way with proceeds of zero, since it has no value: minus the historical cost of its units (see Outgoing Adjustments)
  • Cash pool decomposition: SELL returns \(C = q_{\text{sold}} \times \text{WAC}^{T}_{\text{pre-sell}}\) to Capital Pool
  • Yield on Cost: the average purchase price of the Yield on Cost denominator
  • Transfer form: auto-suggests the receiving side's cost_basis_override from the sending position's WAC

WAC is never a price

WAC is an accounting construct for cost basis. Market value uses the unified resolver tiers: MARKET → TRADE_AVG → CARRIED → MISSING, exposed to portfolio rows as MARKET_PRICE or LAST_TRADE_PRICE. Only a position whose asset has no mark at all — no quote, no BUY or SELL, no transfer cost estimate yet — is counted at its cost basis \(q \times \text{WAC}^{T}\), as a declared estimate with no price and no unrealized P&L (ESTIMATED_AT_COST), or left unvalued (MISSING) when that cost is incomplete. See Price Resolution.

docs.title: ⚙️ Implementation: Position-Level Scope
docs.text:
WAC is maintained per position \((a, b)\) — i.e., per (asset, broker) pair. The same asset held on two brokers has two independent WAC pools.

\[ \text{WAC}(a, b_1, t) \neq \text{WAC}(a, b_2, t) \quad \text{in general} \]

The average cost of every position in a report is computed once, before the daily replay, with all the conversions it needs batched into a single request to the FX service; the daily replay then follows each position's pool step by step instead of recomputing it, and never converts a cost itself.

docs.title: 📅 Same-day transaction ordering
docs.text:
Within the same date, additions are processed before reductions:

\[ \text{BUY}_1, \text{BUY}_2, \ldots \quad \text{then} \quad \text{SELL}_1, \text{SELL}_2, \ldots \]

This prevents transient negative quantities and ensures SELL always reads the correct WAC that includes same-day BUYs.

docs.title: 🔬 FIFO Lot Analysis
docs.text:
FIFO lot analysis is the per-lot complement to Weighted Average Cost (WAC).

WAC answers: "What is my blended average cost for this position?" FIFO lot analysis answers a different question: "How is each individual purchase batch performing through time?"

Instead of merging all acquisitions into one pool, LibreFolio tracks each lot through its own lifecycle — open, partially closed, fully closed — and matches sells in FIFO order (first in, first out).

Complement, not replacement

WAC is aggregate and position-level. FIFO lot analysis is granular and lot-level. Both views are useful: one for blended cost basis, one for economic attribution lot by lot.

docs.title: 💡 What is FIFO Lot Analysis?
docs.text:
A lot is one acquisition batch: for example, one BUY of 100 shares, or one transfer-in that preserves historical cost basis.

When a SELL occurs, the oldest still-open lots are closed first. This creates a lot-by-lot history:

  • how much of each lot is still open
  • how much has already been sold
  • how much sale proceeds that lot has generated
  • how much income was earned while that lot was held
  • how much return came from price change versus cash income

This makes FIFO lot analysis especially useful when two positions in the same asset were bought at very different prices or dates.

The Lot Life & Custody timeline above makes the lifecycle visual: each bar is one lot, colored by the broker currently holding it, with thickness proportional to the quantity still held in that segment. A bar that ends mid-chart is a fully closed lot; a bar reaching "today" is still open.

docs.title: 🧮 Open Return per Lot
docs.text:
Open Return isolates the price-only move of a lot relative to its opening reference price.

\[ \text{RelativeReturn} = \frac{\text{MarketPrice}}{\text{ReferenceUnitPrice}} - 1 \]

\(\text{MarketPrice}\) is the asset's mark from the unified resolver: on the end date for the lot summary, on each day for the return history. The reference depends on what opened the lot:

  • A trade — a BUY, or a SELL that opens a short lot: the lot's own unit price, even when the asset has a market quote that day. A trade is a price.
  • An adjustment — an opening position, a succession, a transfer from an untracked broker: its cost basis is a cost, not a price, so the reference is the asset's mark on the opening day. That is the price of the last day on or before it that has one — its market quote or, without a quote, the average price of its BUY and SELL trades, never an adjustment — carried forward. For an asset with nothing else yet, the cost of an incoming transfer is such a price too, as an estimate: a transfer from a broker outside the scope, on an asset with no quote and no other operation on or before its day, gets its own cost as its reference, flagged as a fallback (REFERENCE_PRICE_FALLBACK).
  • An adjustment before any price — no quote, BUY, SELL or transfer cost estimate on or before its opening day: the lot's own unit price, its per-unit cost basis. Without a cost basis that price is zero, and the lot has no Open Return.

reference_price_source is exact for a market quote of the opening day itself and for the lot's own price, and fallback for a quote carried from an earlier day or a price derived from trades. The data-quality banner reports such a fallback (REFERENCE_PRICE_FALLBACK), and an adjustment with no price on or before its opening day (REFERENCE_PRICE_UNAVAILABLE).

Each price converts into the target currency at the rate of its own day: \(\text{MarketPrice}\) at the rate of the day it values, the reference at the rate of the opening date, even when it was carried from an earlier quote or trade. For a price in another currency than the target, Open Return therefore includes the exchange-rate move since the opening.

This metric excludes dividends, interest, and realized sale proceeds. It answers: "How much has market price moved since this lot was opened?"

A lot received by succession

An asset is quoted at 50 on 7 March and bought at 52 on 9 March, with no quote since. A lot received by succession on 10 March has a reference of 52: the BUY is the asset's most recent price on or before that day, carried forward. Its reference_price_source is fallback, since 52 is not a quote of 10 March; a quote on 10 March itself would be the reference, with exact.

The lot's own price, on the quote axis

When the reference is the lot's own price, LibreFolio scales it to the asset's quote convention. This avoids misleading percentage returns on instruments quoted per 100 nominal units. A mark from the resolver is already on that axis.

The reference is then \(\text{OpeningUnitPrice}\times qbq\). For qbq = 100, a bond bought at 0.992 compares against the market quote axis as 99.20, not 0.992.

The WAC / Market Price chart plots each lot as a bubble against the market price line: bubble color marks the broker where the lot was opened, bubble size scales with the lot's opening value. A lot whose current value is estimated at cost — its asset has no price at all on the end date, see Estimated-at-Cost — is drawn with a dashed outline.

docs.title: 💰 Total Return per Lot
docs.text:
Total Return is broader than Open Return. It includes the lot's remaining market value, any sale proceeds already realized from that lot — an outgoing adjustment adds none, having no value — and any allocated income received while the lot was held.

LibreFolio's lot math uses these exact building blocks:

\[ \text{OpeningValue} = \text{OriginalCost} \] \[ \text{Proceeds}(t) = \sum \text{Closure Proceeds} \text{ up to } t \] \[ \text{TotalValue}(t) = \text{OpenValue}(t) + \text{Proceeds}(t) \] \[ \text{PnL}(t) = \text{TotalValue}(t) - \text{OriginalCost} \] \[ \text{MarketPnL} = \text{PnL} - \text{RealizedPnL} \] \[ \text{RealizedPnL} = \sum \text{Closure Realized PnL} \] \[ \text{AssetIncome} = \sum_t \text{Income}_i(t) \] \[ \text{TotalPnL} = \text{MarketPnL} + \text{RealizedPnL} + \text{AssetIncome} \]

Every amount is in the analysis's target currency. For a lot bought or sold in another currency, each closure converts its two legs at their own dates — see Lots in Another Currency.

For the scalar lot summary, the return percentage is:

\[ \text{TotalReturn} = \frac{\text{TotalPnL}}{\text{OpeningValue}} \]

For return history through time, LibreFolio uses:

\[ \text{TotalReturn}(t) = \frac{\text{TotalValue}(t) + \text{Income}(t)}{\text{OriginalCost}} - 1 \]

This answers: "What is full economic return of this lot, including both price movement and cash yield?"

The Value / Return comparison chart, switched to Return mode, plots exactly this percentage — one line per lot, each measured from its own opening date, over the currently selected lot set.

docs.title: 💱 Lots in Another Currency
docs.text:
A closure's two legs convert into the target currency each in its own currency, at its own date: the cost of the units in the lot's currency at the lot's opening date — the purchase rate — and the closing price in the closing transaction's currency at the closing date — the sale rate. With \(\text{Convert}(x, ccy, D)\) the amount \(x\) in currency \(ccy\) converted into the target currency at the rate of date \(D\), a closure of \(q\) units of a LONG lot opened on \(D_{\text{open}}\) at \(\text{LotUnitCost}\) in \(ccy_{\text{lot}}\), and closed on \(D_{\text{close}}\) at \(\text{ClosePrice}\) in \(ccy_{\text{close}}\), gives:

\[ \text{Closure Proceeds} = \text{Convert}\left(q \cdot \text{ClosePrice},\ ccy_{\text{close}},\ D_{\text{close}}\right) \] \[ \text{Closure Cost} = \text{Convert}\left(q \cdot \text{LotUnitCost},\ ccy_{\text{lot}},\ D_{\text{open}}\right) \] \[ \text{Closure Realized PnL} = \text{Closure Proceeds} - \text{Closure Cost} \]

\(\text{ClosePrice}\) is a sale's unit price, in the sale's currency, or zero, in the lot's currency, for an outgoing adjustment, which has no value (see Outgoing Adjustments). \(ccy_{\text{close}}\) need not be \(ccy_{\text{lot}}\): a lot moved to a broker of another currency and sold there converts the sale from that currency. A SHORT lot mirrors the rule: it realizes the proceeds of its opening sale, \(\text{Convert}(q \cdot \text{LotUnitCost}, ccy_{\text{lot}}, D_{\text{open}})\), minus the cost of the purchase that closes it, \(\text{Convert}(q \cdot \text{ClosePrice}, ccy_{\text{close}}, D_{\text{close}})\).

When a lot is bought and sold in one currency, with rates \(r_{\text{open}}\) and \(r_{\text{close}}\) on the two dates, its realized result splits into the price gain at the sale rate and the exchange-rate move on the cost of the units sold:

\[ \text{Closure Realized PnL} = q\,(\text{ClosePrice} - \text{LotUnitCost})\,r_{\text{close}} + q\,\text{LotUnitCost}\,(r_{\text{close}} - r_{\text{open}}) \]

The exchange-rate move between purchase and sale is therefore realized with the units, as on the Dashboard, where a sale's proceeds convert at its date and the units leave at their historical cost (see WAC). A missing rate leaves the closure's realized P&L unknown, and with it the lot's \(\text{RealizedPnL}\): it is never computed from the native amounts.

Every closure's cost converts at the opening date, like \(\text{OriginalCost}\), so a LONG lot's market P&L is the value of its open units minus their cost at the purchase rate:

\[ \text{MarketPnL} = \text{PnL} - \text{RealizedPnL} = \text{OpenValue} - \left(\text{OriginalCost} - \sum \text{Closure Cost}\right) \]

A fully closed LONG lot has no market P&L: its closures' costs add up to its \(\text{OriginalCost}\), and its whole P&L is realized.

A dollar lot, target currency EUR

Buy 1 unit at 100 USD when 1 USD = 1.00 EUR; sell it at 110 USD when 1 USD = 0.90 EUR.

\[ \text{Closure Proceeds} = 110 \times 0.90 = 99 \text{ EUR} \qquad \text{Closure Cost} = 100 \times 1.00 = 100 \text{ EUR} \] \[ \text{RealizedPnL} = 99 - 100 = -1 \text{ EUR} \qquad \text{MarketPnL} = \text{PnL} - \text{RealizedPnL} = (99 - 100) - (-1) = 0 \]

The price gain, \(10 \times 0.90 = +9\) EUR, is outweighed by the dollar's fall on the cost, \(100 \times (0.90 - 1.00) = -10\) EUR. Converting the native realized P&L, 10 USD, at the sale rate would instead report \(+9\) EUR realized and \(-10\) EUR of market P&L on a lot no longer held; the total, \(-1\) EUR, is the same either way.

docs.title: ⚙️ qbq Scaling
docs.text:
Some instruments are quoted per base quantity, not per single unit. LibreFolio calls this base quantity qbq (quote_base_quantity).

  • For most stocks, qbq = 1
  • For many bonds, qbq = 100

The exact valuation rule is:

\[ \text{HoldingValue}(qty, price, qbq) = \left(\frac{qty}{qbq}\right)\cdot price \] \[ \text{OpenValue}(t) = \left(\frac{\text{OpenQuantity}(t)}{qbq}\right)\cdot \text{MarketPrice}(t) \]

qbq scaling matters

Suppose a bond has face quantity 1,000 and is quoted at 101.50 per 100 nominal.

  • qbq = 100
  • lot quantity = 1,000
  • market value = (1,000 / 100) × 101.50 = 1,015.00

If you compare 101.50 directly with a per-single-unit cost basis such as 0.992, you get nonsense because the two numbers live on different scales.

The correct comparison rescales the lot cost onto the market quote axis:

\[ 0.992 \times 100 = 99.20 \]

So the meaningful price comparison is 101.50 vs 99.20, not 101.50 vs 0.992.

Without this scaling, bond returns and valuations can be off by orders of magnitude.

docs.title: 🛟 Estimated-at-Cost
docs.text:
Each day, a lot is valued at the asset's mark from the unified resolver: a market quote, or the average price of a day's BUY and SELL trades, carried forward. An adjustment is never a price, with or without a cost basis; the cost of an incoming transfer is one only as an estimate, while the asset has no quote and no other operation on or before that day. A day with no price at all — no market quote, no BUY or SELL and no such estimate on or before it — does not fail the analysis: LibreFolio values the still-open portion of a LONG lot at cost that day, the day-by-day rule the Dashboard applies to a holding with no price:

\[ \text{OpenValue}(t) = \text{OpeningValue}\cdot \frac{\text{OpenQuantity}(t)}{\text{OriginalQuantity}} \] \[ \text{MarketPnL}(t) = 0 \]

with \(\text{OpeningValue}\) the lot's original cost converted at its opening date. The choice is made day by day, with no look-ahead. A price, once observed, is carried forward, so these days all come before the asset's first quote, BUY, SELL or transfer cost estimate: they run from the first transaction of the analysis to the day before that first price, or to the end date when the asset has none — and there are none when the asset already has a price on the day of the first transaction.

  • Before the first price. A lot opened before the asset's first price — by an adjustment, for example — is valued at cost from its opening to the day before that price, even when the asset is priced later: its value line stays flat at cost, with no market gain or loss, then follows the price.
  • No price at all. An asset with no quote, BUY, SELL or transfer cost estimate up to the end date — one held only through adjustments, or through transfers without a cost basis — is valued at cost on every day, and the lot summary reports value_source = ESTIMATED_AT_COST. With a price on or before the end date, the summary values the lot at that price instead: value_source = MARKET_PRICE, the label of any mark, quote, trade or transfer cost estimate. An asset that arrived only by transfers with a cost basis therefore has no day at cost: from its first transfer it is valued at that cost, converted at each day's exchange rate, and the price series have a point for it, flagged as estimated.
  • A price without a rate. A day whose mark has no exchange rate into the target currency is not valued at cost: a still-open lot has no value that day, and on the end date the lot summary has no value and no value_source.
  • An adjustment without a cost basis. An adjustment with no cost, such as a gift or a spin-off, opens a zero-cost lot, and that lot is worth 0 on the days valued at cost until a price arrives. It counts at zero on those days, while the Dashboard's average cost treats that cost as unknown and leaves the holding unvalued. Such a row is rare: a positive adjustment can be saved without a cost basis only while it is linked to a split, and then opens no lot, so it comes from an older version, or from one whose split event was later changed to a price adjustment.

Practical implication, on the days valued at cost:

  • the lot still shows residual value
  • already realized proceeds still remain visible
  • allocated dividends or interest still remain visible
  • unrealized volatility is temporarily understated
  • market_pnl = 0, and no Open Return: there is no market price to compare with the reference
  • no ROI or TWRR in the lots performance history, which reads only days with a price

Interpretation

Estimated-at-cost is conservative operational fallback. It means: "We know what you paid, but we do not currently know what market would pay."

The data-quality warning CURRENT_PRICE_ASSUMED_AT_COST — "No market price available between {date_from} and {date_to} — open value estimated at cost, market P&L excluded" — names exactly those days: from the first transaction to the day before the asset's first price, or to the end date when the asset has none. It is raised whenever such days exist and the lot summary or the value, return, price or performance history is requested.

docs.title: 💸 Income Allocation Across Lots
docs.text:
Dividends and interest linked to an asset are allocated pro-rata across the LONG lots that are eligible as of the day before the income date (D-1), and only across lots held at the paying broker.

Exact allocation rule:

\[ w_i(D) = \frac{\text{EligibleQty}_i(D)}{\sum_j \text{EligibleQty}_j(D)}, \qquad \text{EligibleQty}_i(D) = \text{OpenQty}_i(D-1) \] \[ \text{Income}_i = \text{Convert}(I, ccy, D)\cdot w_i(D) \]

Where:

  • \(I\) = income amount received on date \(D\)
  • \(\text{Convert}(I, ccy, D)\) = income converted into target currency on date \(D\)
  • \(\text{EligibleQty}_i(D)\) = quantity of lot \(i\) open at the paying broker on \(D-1\) (quantity that left that broker in transit still counts as originating there)
  • only LONG lots participate in the denominator

The D-1 rule keeps the day of record clean: a purchase made on the income date does not earn that distribution, and a lot sold the day before does not either. Larger eligible lots receive a larger share; lots held at other brokers, or not yet (or no longer) eligible, receive nothing.

Income keeps its sign: a negative correction of a dividend or interest payment lowers the lot's income, as it does on the Dashboard.

Changed in FIFO v5

Earlier versions used the income date itself with all brokers (\(\text{OpenQty}_i(t)\) over every lot). The current engine uses D-1 eligibility scoped to the paying broker. If no lot is eligible, the income is kept as asset-level orphan income (never dropped, never assigned to the wrong lot).

Conservation rule

The allocated lot amounts add back exactly to the converted income event total. Income is distributed, not created.

The lot detail modal's Asset Income row is exactly \(\text{Income}_i\) from the formula above — the pro-rata slice this specific lot received. When the lot's current value is estimated at cost — its asset has no price at all on the end date —, the same modal also shows the Estimated-at-Cost badge from the previous section.

docs.title: 💸 Costs & Net Metrics
docs.text: Asset-linked FEE and TAX are allocated to lots with a deterministic operation-matching ladder, then subtracted to produce net figures alongside the gross ones.

docs.title: 🧭 Deterministic cost allocation
docs.text:
A cost pool (same broker, same day, same type) is matched to the first non-empty target in this order:

Cost Matching order FEE same-day trades → previous-day trades → open holdings → asset orphan TAX same-day income → same-day trades → previous-day income → previous-day trades → open holdings → asset orphan

Within a matched trade the cost crosses to the very lots that trade touched — a BUY's cost lands on the lot it opened, a SELL's cost lands on the FIFO-consumed lots — so cost attribution never contradicts the FIFO matching itself. Amounts are converted to the target currency and stored as positive magnitudes.

Conservation

Per pool, \(\sum_i \text{Cost}_i + \text{Orphan} = \text{Convert}(\text{pool}, ccy, D)\). A cost that finds no eligible lot (e.g. a fee booked after the position is fully closed) becomes asset-level orphan cost rather than being dropped or forced onto an unrelated lot.

docs.title: ⚖️ Gross vs net
docs.text:
With costs attributed per lot, LibreFolio reports both gross and net performance:

\[ \text{NetTotalPnL}_i = \text{TotalPnL}_i - \text{Fees}_i - \text{Taxes}_i \] \[ \text{NetTotalReturn}_i = \frac{\text{NetTotalPnL}_i}{\text{OpeningValue}_i} \]

where \(\text{TotalPnL}_i\) already includes income (market P&L + realized P&L + asset income). The per-lot value-history series instead reports a capital-only net P&L, \(\text{pnl}_i - \text{Fees}_i - \text{Taxes}_i\), which excludes income — each net line mirrors its own gross counterpart minus costs.

Annualized lot return uses the net return, not the gross one:

\[ \mathrm{AnnualizedReturn}_i = \left(1+\mathrm{NetTotalReturn}_i\right)^{365/d_i}-1 \]

with \(d_i\) from opening date to closing date for closed lots, or to the analysis end date for open lots. Windows below 30 days return no annualized value; see Net Annualized Return.

Canonical numbers

BUY 10×100, SELL 4×120, current price 110, dividend 50, fees 8, taxes 5: Gross Total P&L \(= 60 + 80 + 50 = 190\); Net Total P&L \(= 190 - 13 = 177\); on opening value 1000 that is a 19% gross vs 17.7% net total return.

Costs with asset_id = null are not part of this lot-level view — they are portfolio-level and handled by the Portfolio Engine. See Fee & Tax for the instrument-level theory.

docs.title: 📝 Worked Example
docs.text:
Example: two lots, one dividend, one market price

Assume same stock, same currency, qbq = 1.

Date Event Lot A Open Qty Lot B Open Qty Notes Jan 2 BUY 100 @ $10 100 0 Lot A opens with original cost $1,000 Feb 10 BUY 50 @ $14 100 50 Lot B opens with original cost $700 Mar 15 DIVIDEND $30 100 50 Both lots are still open Apr 1 Market price = $16 100 50 Evaluate both lots

Step 1 — Allocate dividend pro-rata

\[ w_A = \frac{100}{100 + 50} = \frac{2}{3} \qquad w_B = \frac{50}{100 + 50} = \frac{1}{3} \] \[ \text{Income}_A = 30 \times \frac{2}{3} = 20 \qquad \text{Income}_B = 30 \times \frac{1}{3} = 10 \]

Step 2 — Open Return for each lot

\[ \text{RelativeReturn}_A = \frac{16}{10} - 1 = 60.00\% \] \[ \text{RelativeReturn}_B = \frac{16}{14} - 1 \approx 14.29\% \]

Step 3 — Market value and Total Return

\[ \text{OpenValue}_A = 100 \times 16 = 1,600 \qquad \text{OpenValue}_B = 50 \times 16 = 800 \]

Since no shares were sold yet, proceeds and realized P&L are both zero.

\[ \text{TotalPnL}_A = (1,600 - 1,000) + 20 = 620 \] \[ \text{TotalReturn}_A = \frac{620}{1,000} = 62.00\% \] \[ \text{TotalPnL}_B = (800 - 700) + 10 = 110 \] \[ \text{TotalReturn}_B = \frac{110}{700} \approx 15.71\% \]

Step 4 — Aggregate return across displayed lots

\[ \text{AggregateReturn} = \frac{620 + 110}{1,000 + 700} = \frac{730}{1,700} \approx 42.94\% \]

Even though both lots belong to same asset, their returns differ because they were opened at different prices.

docs.title: 📚 From Lots to Aggregate Metrics
docs.text:
Lot-level returns can be rolled up into an aggregate return series, but percentages must not be added directly.

LibreFolio uses this exact aggregate rule across displayed lots:

\[ \text{AggregatePnL}(t) = \sum_i \left(\text{PnL}_i(t) + \text{Income}_i(t)\right) \] \[ \text{AggregateOpeningValue}(t) = \sum_i \text{OriginalCost}_i \] \[ \text{AggregateReturn}(t) = \frac{\text{AggregatePnL}(t)}{\text{AggregateOpeningValue}(t)} \]

This lot-level view helps explain where return came from. Higher-level metrics such as ROI and TWRR answer broader portfolio questions:

  • ROI focuses on gain relative to invested capital
  • TWRR neutralizes external cash-flow timing
  • FIFO lot analysis explains contribution and path inside a position

Price lookup is deliberately outside the FIFO engine itself. The engine produces lots and closures, and asks for a price only to give a lot opened by an adjustment its reference; LotsAnalysisService answers from the unified resolver (Price Resolution), then applies the same resolver and the estimated-at-cost fallback when deriving valuation metrics.

The Unified Lots Table lists exactly the per-lot rows \(i\) that the aggregate formulas above sum over — opening date, total return, current value, custody, and status, all filterable to the same visible lot set used by the charts.

docs.title: 🧬 FIFO Engine — Lot Lifecycle & Matching Model
💡 Overview
docs.text:
While Weighted Average Cost blends every acquisition of a position into one running average, LibreFolio's FIFO engine keeps track of individual lots — one per acquisition batch — through their entire lifecycle: opening, partial closures, transfers between brokers, splits, and eventual full closure.

This page describes the mechanics of that engine: how lots are created, matched, and closed. For the metrics derived from this engine (Open/Total Return, qbq scaling, income allocation, a worked example), see FIFO Lot Analysis.

The FIFO engine is price-feed-independent. It replays quantities, lots, fragments, transfers, and realized closures. Current valuation tiers live outside it: Price Resolution and LotsAnalysisService supply reference/current marks and estimated-at-cost behavior.

Two engines, two questions

Portfolio Engine (WAC-based) answers: "What is my blended cost basis for this position?"

FIFO Engine answers a structurally different question: "Which specific batch of units am I selling, and how did that exact batch perform?"

docs.title: 🧱 What is a Lot?
docs.text:
A lot is one economic acquisition batch for one asset: a single BUY, the open remainder of an inventory adjustment, or a transfer-in that preserves its original cost basis. A lot keeps its own identity for its entire life, even as it moves between brokers or splits into pieces.

Property Meaning Direction LONG (bought first) or SHORT (sold first, only where the broker allows shorting) Opening date & broker Where and when the lot came into existence Original quantity & cost Fixed at opening, later rescaled only by splits — never by transfers Open quantity How much of the lot has not yet been matched by an opposite transaction Custody Which broker (or brokers, over time) currently holds the open quantity Reference price reference_unit_price plus reference_price_source (exact, fallback, unavailable) for open-return comparisons

docs.title: 🔁 Lot Lifecycle States
docs.text:
State Meaning OPEN Nothing has been matched yet — the full original quantity is still held PARTIALLY_CLOSED Some, but not all, of the lot has been matched by later opposite transactions CLOSED The entire lot has been matched — nothing remains open

A lot moves OPEN → PARTIALLY_CLOSED → CLOSED strictly forward in time as matching consumes it; it never reopens. Independently of this lifecycle, a lot can also be tagged:

  • IN_TRANSIT — part of its open quantity is currently mid-transfer between brokers
  • DISTRIBUTED — its open quantity is currently split across more than one custody location at once
  • DEGRADED — a data-quality issue was recorded against this specific lot (see Data Quality below)

docs.title: 📅 Chronological Event Processing
docs.text:
LibreFolio replays every transaction for an asset in chronological order, classifying each into one event kind:

Event Effect BUY First closes any open SHORT lots on that broker; any remainder opens a new LONG lot SELL Closes open LONG lots in FIFO order on that broker; any remainder opens a new SHORT lot only where the broker allows shorting Adjustment in Same matching logic as BUY, at the adjustment's per-unit cost basis (zero without one): any remainder opens a new LONG lot at that cost — in the cost basis's currency when it has one Adjustment out Closes open LONG lots in FIFO order on that broker, like a SELL, at zero: it has no value, so each lot realizes minus the cost of the units it gives up; it never opens a SHORT lot SPLIT Rescales quantity and unit cost for every open lot of the asset Transfer (depart / arrive) Moves custody of a lot's open quantity from one broker to another

Same-day ordering

When several events fall on the same date, LibreFolio always processes them in a fixed order — transfer departures, then transfer arrivals, then splits, then ordinary buys/sells/adjustments — so that same-day transfers and splits always see a consistent custody state.

docs.title: ⛏️ FIFO Matching
docs.text:
When a closing event (a SELL, or the opposite-direction leg of an adjustment) needs to consume a quantity \(Q\), LibreFolio always matches against the oldest still-open lot first, on that same broker:

\[ \text{MatchOrder} = \text{sort by } (\text{OpeningDate}, \text{LotId}) \]

It walks this ordered list, closing quantity from the oldest lot until \(Q\) is fully matched, only moving to the next-oldest lot once the current one is exhausted. Realized profit or loss is computed per matched piece, using the price carried by the exact lot fragment consumed:

\[ \text{RealizedPnL}_{\text{LONG}} = \text{MatchedQuantity} \times (\text{ClosePrice} - \text{LotUnitCost}) \] \[ \text{RealizedPnL}_{\text{SHORT}} = \text{MatchedQuantity} \times (\text{LotUnitCost} - \text{ClosePrice}) \]

\(\text{ClosePrice}\) is the trade's unit price for a SELL, or for a BUY closing a SHORT lot. An adjustment trades nothing: an incoming one closes at its per-unit cost basis override, or at zero without one. An outgoing adjustment has no value: it always closes at zero, so every lot it consumes realizes minus the cost of those units, whatever cost basis the row holds (see Outgoing Adjustments).

This is why two lots of the same asset, bought at different times and prices, can show very different realized results even though they are later matched on the same day at the same price — see the worked example in FIFO Lot Analysis.

Both formulas take the two prices in the lot's own currency. In the analysis's target currency, each leg of the closure converts at its own date — the lot's cost at the opening date, the closing price, in its own currency, at the closing date — and the realized P&L is their difference (see Lots in Another Currency).

docs.title: ✂️ Splits — Quantity/Price Rescaling
docs.text:
A stock split (or reverse split) with ratio \(r\) rescales every currently open fragment of every affected lot:

\[ \text{NewQuantity} = \text{Quantity} \times r \qquad \text{NewUnitCost} = \frac{\text{UnitCost}}{r} \]

The economic cost of the position is invariant across a split — only quantity and per-unit cost move, in opposite directions, so \(\text{Quantity} \times \text{UnitCost}\) stays constant for every lot.

Reference prices are rescaled with open quantity when splits alter the lot quantity, preserving comparison on the post-split unit axis.

docs.title: 🚚 Transfers — Custody Movement, Not a Sale
docs.text:
A transfer between brokers is modeled as a custody change, never as a disposal:

  • Depart — LibreFolio extracts the transferred quantity from the source broker in FIFO order. If the transfer takes more than one day to settle, it opens a temporary in-transit custody fragment in the meantime.
  • Arrive — On arrival, the in-transit fragment closes and an equivalent fragment reopens at the destination broker, carrying over the same quantity and unit cost.

The lot's identity, opening date, and original cost never change because of a transfer — only where it is currently held. No profit or loss is ever realized by a transfer.

This custody history — which broker (or in transit) held a lot's open quantity, and how much, at every point in time — is exactly what powers the Lot Life & Custody timeline in the FIFO Lots Analysis panel: each bar segment is colored by the custody broker holding it, and its thickness reflects the quantity held during that segment.

docs.title: ⚠️ Data Quality: Best-Effort, Not All-or-Nothing
docs.text:
If the transaction history contains something the engine cannot fully resolve — for example a closing transaction with no matching open lot on that broker, or a transfer whose paired leg is missing — LibreFolio does not abort the whole calculation. It records the specific issue, marks the affected lot(s) as degraded, and continues processing the rest of the history with the best available data.

The overall result is then marked complete or degraded as a whole, but charts and tables built on a degraded result still render normally for every lot that was not affected. You may see this reflected as a data-quality banner in the FIFO Lots Analysis panel.

docs.title: 💡 What is Book Value?
docs.text: Book Value represents the historical accounting cost of your portfolio — open cost basis plus cash reserves and in-transit book value. It does not fluctuate with market prices — only cash held in another currency follows its exchange rate, in Book as in NAV — and it is distinct from Price Resolution.

docs.title: 🧮 Formula
docs.text:
\[ \boxed{\mathrm{Book}(t) = \mathrm{OCB}(t) + \mathrm{Cash}(t) + \mathrm{InTransitBook}(t)} \]

Where Open Cost Basis:

\[ \mathrm{OCB}(t) = \sum_{\substack{(a,b) \in S \\ q > 10^{-5}}} q(a,b,t) \cdot w^{C^*}(a,b,t) \]

The sum runs over the positions held: a position left with \(10^{-5}\) units or fewer is not held (Portfolio Engine — §3). Here \(w^{C^*}(a,b,t)\) is the WAC kept directly in the requested currency \(C^*\): each acquisition entered it at the rate of its own date \(d_i\), as \(P_i \cdot \mathrm{fx}(\mathrm{ccy}(P_i), C^*, d_i)\) for an amount \(P_i\) actually paid. OCB therefore uses no exchange rate at the valuation date \(t\): it is the sum of historical costs — what was paid — and it does not move when exchange rates move.

Cash, instead, is each broker's cash kept in the currencies it was recorded in and valued at the rate of \(t\):

\[ \mathrm{Cash}(t) = \sum_{b \in S} \sum_{c} N_{b,c}(t) \cdot \mathrm{fx}(c, C^*, t) \]

Here \(N_{b,c}(t)\) is the balance broker \(b\) holds in currency \(c\) on \(t\) — its movements in \(c\) dated on or before \(t\), scaled by the broker's ownership share — and \(\mathrm{fx}(c, C^*, t)\) is the latest rate on or before \(t\), with \(\mathrm{fx}(C^*, C^*, t) = 1\). Unlike OCB, Cash moves with exchange rates: 1,000 USD are worth €900 at 0.90 EUR per USD and €950 at 0.95. Each movement was still booked at the rate of its own date, and the capital flows among them entered the capital baseline at that rate; only the balance held afterwards follows the rate.

In the in-transit term, cash in transit is converted at \(t\) too, like the cash at rest, while assets in transit carry their frozen cost converted at their arrival date.

Incomplete cost

When part of a position's cost is unknown — no exchange rate on or before an acquisition date, or a transfer or adjustment without cost basis — OCB includes only the known part, and the position itself is flagged: its average cost and unrealized gain/loss are not shown.

🔗 See Portfolio Engine — §3 Position State for full derivation.

docs.title: ⚖️ Unrealized Gain/Loss
docs.text:
\[ \mathrm{Unrealized}(t) = \mathrm{NAV}(t) - \mathrm{Book}(t) \]

Because NAV values the assets at the day's market price and exchange rate while Book keeps historical costs, the unrealized gain/loss of an asset priced in another currency includes the effect of the exchange rate. For example, 10 units bought for €400 when they were worth 500 USD keep an OCB of €400; if they are worth 550 USD on a day when 1 USD = €0.75, their market value is €412.50 and the unrealized gain is €12.50 — the units' own gain (+€37.50) less the dollar's fall (−€25.00). Period P&L shows how the Dashboard splits the two.

Cash held in another currency is different: \(\mathrm{Cash}(t)\) is the same term in NAV and in Book, valued at the rate of \(t\) on both sides, so its exchange-rate effect cancels in the difference and Unrealized excludes it. It is a result all the same: the engine books it as the exchange result on cash, it is part of the Total P&L, and over a period it is the FX on cash part of Other. For example, 1,000 USD deposited at 0.90 EUR per USD and held while the rate rises to 0.95 count €950 in both NAV and Book: Unrealized does not move, while the Total P&L gains €50 over the €900 of capital.

docs.title: 📝 Example
docs.text:
Component Amount Open Cost Basis €27,000 Cash €600 In-Transit Book €0 \[ \mathrm{Book} = 27\,000 + 600 = 27\,600 \text{ EUR} \]

With NAV = €33,000:

\[ \mathrm{Unrealized} = 33\,000 - 27\,600 = +5\,400 \text{ EUR} \]

docs.title: 💸 Deposited Capital, Total PnL and Cash Pools
💡 Concept Overview
docs.text:
Capital Baseline = cumulative economic capital contributed since inception:

\[ \mathrm{CapitalBaseline}(t)= \sum_{\tau \leq t}\mathrm{ExternalCashFlow}(\tau) + \sum_{\tau \leq t}\mathrm{InKindCapital}(\tau) \]

Total PnL = all value generated above external contributions:

\[ \boxed{\mathrm{TotalPnL}(t) = \mathrm{NAV}(t) - \mathrm{CapitalBaseline}(t)} \]

InKindCapital covers the securities that enter or leave the scope without cash:

  • incoming ADJUSTMENT rows carrying a cost basis (cost_basis_override, not linked to a split), at cost: the cost they add to the position; an outgoing row never counts: it has no value (Outgoing Adjustments);
  • TRANSFER legs whose other leg is not in the scope — it sits at a broker outside the view, is missing, or was never linked — at market value on their own date: \(+\) for securities received, \(-\) for securities sent. A received leg with a cost basis, for a security with no quote and no other operation on or before its date, gives the security its price: its own cost, as an estimate, so on its date its market value is that cost and the leg is neutral. A security with no price at all on that date — no quote, no BUY or SELL and no such estimate on or before it — counts at cost instead: the cost the leg moves in its position, the cost a received leg adds or the average cost a sent leg removes. An unknown cost counts as zero, as in the position's own cost. While the position's cost is complete, the NAV values the holding at that same cost and the leg is neutral; with part of the cost unknown, the holding has no value in the NAV, yet the leg still moves its known cost, so nothing is left in the capital once the units are gone. Nothing counts if the security cannot be valued that day: it has a price, but the exchange rate is missing.

These rows move value without cash: they are capital, not profit or loss. An outgoing ADJUSTMENT is not capital: it realizes the average cost its position gives up as a loss.

docs.title: 🎯 What Counts
docs.text: Transaction Effect on capital baseline DEPOSIT / WITHDRAWAL (unlinked) ✅ Yes CASH_TRANSFER / FX_CONVERSION whose other leg is outside the view, missing, or never linked (orphan) ✅ Yes, at its amount, like a deposit or a withdrawal CASH_TRANSFER / FX_CONVERSION / TRANSFER with both legs in the view (internal pair) ❌ No. Per broker, a pair across two brokers moves capital from the sender to the receiver on the arrival day, summing to zero (Internal Transfers) TRANSFER of securities whose other leg is outside the view, missing, or never linked (orphan) ✅ Yes, in-kind capital at market value on its date, or at cost for a security with no price at all Incoming ADJUSTMENT with cost_basis_override, not split-linked ✅ Yes, in-kind capital at cost Outgoing ADJUSTMENT ❌ No: it has no value, and realizes the cost of its units as a loss (below) SPLIT-linked ADJUSTMENT ❌ No, quantity rescale only BUY, SELL, DIVIDEND, INTEREST, FEE, TAX ❌ No Exchange-rate move on cash held in another currency (no transaction) ❌ No: a result, part of TotalPnL; the capital flows (deposits, withdrawals, orphan cash legs) entered the baseline at the rate of their own dates

docs.title: 📤 Outgoing Adjustments
docs.text:
An ADJUSTMENT that removes \(|q|\) units of asset \(a\) from broker \(b\) on date \(d\) — units given away, sent to an account LibreFolio does not track, or removed by a correction — has no value, whatever cost basis the row holds: it only lowers the quantity. The position gives up the historical cost of those units, at its average cost before the adjustment, each purchase at the rate of its own date, and nothing comes back:

\[ C = s_b \cdot |q| \cdot w_{\text{pre}}(a,b) \] \[ \Delta\mathrm{CapitalBaseline}(d) = 0, \qquad \mathrm{Realized} = -C \]

\(s_b\) is the broker's ownership share.

  • Capital. Nothing leaves the capital baseline, nor the capital of broker \(b\)'s line. No cash moves, so the cash pools do not change.
  • Realized. \(-C\) counts in the period's realized gain or loss and in the position's contribution (Period P&L), and is left out, as a sale is, when the position's cost is incomplete. The average cost of the units that remain does not change.
  • Returns. TWRR and MWRR take their flows from the changes of the capital baseline, so the adjustment is no flow: the value of the units leaves the NAV, and the day's return reads it as a loss.

A split-linked ADJUSTMENT is the exception (table above): it only rescales the quantity. Units that leave for money are a SELL.

Two shares given away

Report currency EUR, share 100%. A deposit of €500 buys 10 shares at €50; the price rises to €80. An ADJUSTMENT of −2 shares gives two away, the price unchanged that day: \(C = 2 \times 50 = 100\).

Moment NAV CapitalBaseline TotalPnL Realized Before the adjustment 800 500 +300 0 After the adjustment 640 500 +140 −100

The 8 shares left keep an average cost of €50, so their unrealized gain is \(8 \times (80 - 50) = 240\), and \(-100 + 240 = +140\). The day's flow is 0, so the TWRR reads \(640 / 800 - 1 = -20\%\) that day.

docs.title: 🔀 Internal Transfers in the Broker Lines
docs.text:
With two or more brokers in scope, the P&L chart draws one line per broker. Each broker \(b \in S\) has its own NAV, capital and PnL:

\[ \mathrm{PnL}_b(t) = \mathrm{NAV}_b(t) - C_b(t) \] \[ \mathrm{NAV}_b(t) = \mathrm{MV}_b(t) + \mathrm{Cash}_b(t) + \mathrm{InTransit}_b(t) \] \[ C_b(t) = \sum_{\tau \leq t}\mathrm{ExternalCashFlow}_b(\tau) + \sum_{\tau \leq t}\mathrm{InKindCapital}_b(\tau) + \sum_{\tau \leq t}\mathrm{Internal}_b(\tau) \]

\(\mathrm{InTransit}_b\) is the value in transit that left \(b\), and \(\mathrm{Internal}_b\) is \(b\)'s side of the internal transfers described below. Since \(\sum_b \mathrm{NAV}_b = \mathrm{NAV}\) and the internal flows cancel out every day, the lines add up to the scope figures:

\[ \sum_{b \in S}\mathrm{Internal}_b(t) = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \sum_{b \in S} C_b(t) = \mathrm{CapitalBaseline}(t), \qquad \sum_{b \in S}\mathrm{PnL}_b(t) = \mathrm{TotalPnL}(t) \]

A broker's line is therefore the PnL earned while the value was at that broker, or travelling from it. It is not the unrealized gain of the positions the broker holds.

docs.title: 📐 The Internal Flow
docs.text:
An internal pair is a linked CASH_TRANSFER, FX_CONVERSION or TRANSFER whose two legs are both in \(S\), on two different brokers: the sender \(A\) (the leg going out) and the receiver \(B\) (the leg coming in). It produces one flow, on the arrival day \(t_{arr}\), the date of the later leg:

\[ \mathrm{Internal}_A(t_{arr}) = -X, \qquad \mathrm{Internal}_B(t_{arr}) = +X, \qquad X = s_A \cdot V(t_{arr}) \]

\(s_A\) is the sender's ownership share and \(V(t_{arr})\) the full value the arrival brings to \(B\) that day, valued exactly as the NAV values it:

Pair \(V(t_{arr})\) CASH_TRANSFER The amount received, converted at \(\mathrm{fx}(c, C^*, t_{arr})\) FX_CONVERSION across brokers The received leg, converted the same way: \(-1{,}000\) USD at \(A\) → \(+900\) EUR at \(B\) gives \(V = 900\) EUR, and the conversion cost stays in \(A\)'s line TRANSFER of securities \(\mathrm{MV}\) of the quantity received at the valuation price of \(t_{arr}\), the last known price carried forward if there is none that day. With no price at all on or before \(t_{arr}\), the cost basis the units add to \(B\)'s position — the cost recorded on \(B\)'s leg, converted at that leg's date —, since the NAV values a holding with no price at its cost (§3)

With equal shares, \(X\) is exactly what the arrival adds to \(\mathrm{NAV}_B\), so neither line jumps. The scope's \(\mathrm{CapitalBaseline}\) is untouched, because an internal move is not external capital: NAV, CapitalBaseline, TotalPnL and its candles, ROI, TWRR, MWRR and cash are the same as without the flow. Only the split of the baseline among the brokers changes.

docs.title: ✈️ Value in Transit
docs.text:
When the legs fall on different days, the value travels from the departure day \(t_{dep}\) to the day before \(t_{arr}\). Meanwhile it is part of \(\mathrm{InTransit}_A\), at the sender's share \(s_A\), valued every day: cash at that day's exchange rate, securities at that day's valuation price (at the cost recorded on the transfer if the security has no price at all). No flow happens while the value travels, so its price and exchange-rate moves stay in \(A\)'s line, the arrival day's own move included; \(B\)'s line starts from the value received.

For example, \(A\) receives a deposit of 1,000 USD on day 0 at 0.90 EUR per USD (\(C_A = 900\)) and sends the dollars on day 1; \(B\) receives them on day 4. With the rate at 0.90, 0.91, 0.92, 0.93 on days 1–4, \(A\)'s line reads 0, +10, +20, +30 and \(B\)'s stays at 0. On day 4, \(X = 930\) and \(C_A = 900 - 930 = -30\). Once arrived, the dollars are \(B\)'s cash, revalued every day, so from day 5 \(B\)'s line moves with the rate: at 0.94, it reads +10.

docs.title: 🧩 Special Cases
docs.text:
• Different ownership shares. \(X\) uses \(s_A\), like the value in transit, while the arrival adds \(s_B \cdot V(t_{arr})\) to \(\mathrm{NAV}_B\). \(B\)'s line keeps a residual step of \((s_B - s_A)\,V(t_{arr})\) on the arrival day, and TotalPnL shows the same step, with or without the flow.
  • Value unknown on the arrival day. If \(V(t_{arr})\) cannot be computed — an exchange rate is missing, or the security has no observation on or before \(t_{arr}\) (\(\operatorname{mark} = \varnothing\)) and the cost on \(B\)'s leg is unknown (no cost basis, or one with no exchange rate), so that the arrival adds nothing to \(B\)'s position cost — then \(X = 0\). Nothing is guessed: the jump stays, and the security's value appears in the line of the broker holding it from its first price.
  • No price at all. A security with no observation on or before \(t_{arr}\) moves at the cost its arrival adds to \(B\)'s position — the cost recorded on \(B\)'s leg, the sender's average cost when the transfer is saved with an automatic cost basis — whether or not \(B\)'s cost is complete. With \(B\)'s cost complete, that is the value \(\mathrm{NAV}_B\) takes the units at, so with equal shares \(B\)'s line does not jump. The cost need not equal the value the units had at \(A\) before leaving, \(A\)'s own cost basis or nothing when that cost was incomplete; the difference ends up in \(A\)'s line, and TotalPnL shows it too. With \(B\)'s cost incomplete — \(B\) already held units of unknown cost — \(B\)'s holding has no value in the NAV, which is incomplete: \(B\)'s line takes the gap, its own unknown cost, and \(A\)'s line is the same as with a complete cost at \(B\).
  • Fees. They are not part of \(X\). A FEE row of 5 recorded at the sender, or the same 5 as a gap between the legs (\(-1{,}000\) sent, \(+995\) received, so \(X = 995\)), stays in \(A\)'s line as a loss of 5.
  • Same-broker pairs. Two legs on the same broker, such as a currency conversion inside one account, need no flow: the value never leaves the line.
  • ADJUSTMENT pairs. They are not internal pairs: each leg follows its own rule (see the table above). The receiver's capital rises by the cost its leg adds; the sender's leg has no value, so its capital does not move and it realizes its average cost as a loss (Outgoing Adjustments). With the setup of the example below and both legs on day 2, the receiving leg at a cost of 10: \(A\)'s line drops to \(-100\) and \(B\)'s reads \(+20\), so TotalPnL falls from \(+20\) to \(-80\). To move units between two brokers without that loss, link the two adjustments as a TRANSFER pair.

docs.title: 🔍 Filtered Views
docs.text:
In a view with only some brokers, a TRANSFER leg whose other leg is outside \(S\) — or missing, or never linked — cannot form an internal pair. It is in-kind capital at market value on its own date: \(+\mathrm{MV}\) for securities received, \(-\mathrm{MV}\) for securities sent, at that broker's share — at cost for a security with no price at all, as above — and nothing if the security cannot be valued that day. Unlike an internal flow, it moves the view's CapitalBaseline, so the view's TotalPnL, ROI, TWRR and MWRR treat it as capital, like an in-kind ADJUSTMENT. A CASH_TRANSFER or FX_CONVERSION leg in the same position is external cash at its amount, like a deposit or a withdrawal, and it moves the cash pools as that deposit or withdrawal would: the split of the view's cash between contributed capital and generated returns, and the funding of its later purchases, follow it.

When the broker holding the other leg is deleted, the remaining leg becomes what a split of the pair leaves, and the legs older versions left are converted the same way at startup: securities become an ADJUSTMENT — a received leg in-kind capital at cost when it carries a cost basis (table above), no longer at market value; a sent leg an outgoing ADJUSTMENT without a value, which realizes the cost of its units as a loss (Outgoing Adjustments) — and cash a DEPOSIT or a WITHDRAWAL. The converted rows follow the same rules in every view, the full one included.

Comparing a broker's own view with the combined view:

  • The receiver alone matches its combined line. In \(B\)'s own view the received securities are capital at their market value on \(t_{arr}\), which is the \(X\) of the combined view. This holds with equal shares and a price that both views can see: a price that comes only from trades at \(A\) is not visible in \(B\)'s own view.
  • The sender alone loses the moves in transit. In \(A\)'s own view its capital drops on the departure day by \(s_A \cdot V(t_{dep})\), while in the combined view the value stays with \(A\) until it arrives.

Writing \(\mathrm{PnL}_A^{(S)}\) for \(A\)'s line in the view of scope \(S\), from the departure day on:

\[ \mathrm{PnL}_A^{(A)}(t) = \mathrm{PnL}_A^{(A,B)}(t) - s_A\bigl[V(\min(t, t_{arr})) - V(t_{dep})\bigr] \]

docs.title: 📦 Example — Securities in Transit
docs.text:
All amounts in EUR, shares 100%. \(A\) receives a deposit of 100 and buys 10 units at 10 on day 0. The price is 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15 on days 0–5. \(A\) sends the 10 units on day 1, and \(B\) receives them on day 3.

Combined view (both brokers in \(S\)):

Day Price \(\mathrm{NAV}_A\) \(C_A\) \(\mathrm{PnL}_A\) \(\mathrm{NAV}_B\) \(C_B\) \(\mathrm{PnL}_B\) TotalPnL 0 10 100 100 0 0 0 0 0 1 11 110 (in transit) 100 +10 0 0 0 +10 2 12 120 (in transit) 100 +20 0 0 0 +20 3 13 0 −30 +30 130 130 0 +30 4 14 0 −30 +30 140 130 +10 +40 5 15 0 −30 +30 150 130 +20 +50

On day 3 the flow \(X = 10 \times 13 = 130\) moves capital from \(A\) to \(B\). \(A\) keeps the +30 earned while the units were at \(A\) or travelling (10 → 13), and \(B\) earns from 13 on. \(C_A\) turns negative because \(A\) passed on more value (130) than the capital it took in (100): the difference is its gain. TotalPnL is the same with or without the flow; without it, on day 3 \(A\)'s line would drop to \(0 - 100 = -100\) and \(B\)'s would jump to \(130 - 0 = +130\).

Single-broker views:

Day \(B\) alone: \(C_B\) \(B\) alone: \(\mathrm{PnL}_B\) \(A\) alone: \(C_A\) \(A\) alone: \(\mathrm{PnL}_A\) 0 — — 100 0 1 — — −10 +10 2 — — −10 +10 3 130 0 −10 +10 4 130 +10 −10 +10 5 130 +20 −10 +10

\(B\)'s own view starts at its first transaction and matches \(B\) in the combined view. In \(A\)'s own view the units leave on day 1 at \(10 \times 11 = 110\), so \(C_A = 100 - 110 = -10\) and the line stays at +10: the move from 11 to 13 while travelling is not in it, and \(+30 - (130 - 110) = +10\). Counted as a gain or a loss instead of capital, the same transfer would put \(A\) alone at −100 from day 1 and \(B\) alone at +130 on day 3.

docs.title: 💶 Example — Cash Between Two Brokers
docs.text:
\(A\) receives a deposit of 5,000. Later, \(A\) sends 1,000 to \(B\), both legs on the same day.

Case \(\mathrm{NAV}_A\) \(C_A\) \(\mathrm{PnL}_A\) \(\mathrm{NAV}_B\) \(C_B\) \(\mathrm{PnL}_B\) TotalPnL After the deposit 5,000 5,000 0 0 0 0 0 After the transfer 4,000 4,000 0 1,000 1,000 0 0 \(B\) receives 995 (fee 5) 4,000 4,005 −5 995 995 0 −5 \(B\) owned at 50% 4,000 4,000 0 500 1,000 −500 −500 Without the flow 4,000 5,000 −1,000 1,000 0 +1,000 0

The last row is the same transfer read without the internal flow: the move looks like a loss for \(A\) and a gain for \(B\). With \(B\) owned at 50%, the step of −500 is the residual \((s_B - s_A)\,V = (0.5 - 1) \times 1{,}000\), and TotalPnL shows it too.

docs.title: 📊 Three-Pool Cash Model
docs.text:
The Growth Chart decomposes current cash into two visible aggregates plus a hidden global tracker:

\[ \mathrm{Cash}(t) \approx \sum_b K_b(t) + \sum_b R_b(t) \] Pool Scope Meaning \(K_b\) Per-broker External capital still at broker \(b\) \(R_b\) Per-broker Generated returns still at broker \(b\) \(W\) Global Returns that left the system (restorable on re-deposit)

Key properties

  • \(\mathrm{CapitalBaseline}\) = historical sum of cash and in-kind capital flows. \(\sum K_b\) = how much current cash is external capital. They diverge after BUY/SELL.
  • A BUY on broker \(b_1\) only consumes \(R_{b_1}\), never \(R_{b_2}\).
  • Cash transfers between brokers and currency conversions with both legs in the scope move \(R\) and \(K\) from source to destination without touching \(W\): the departure leaves returns first, and the arrival brings back what it took from capital and returns; any gap between the two legs — another currency, another day's rate, another ownership share — is a result.
  • A cash transfer or conversion leg whose other leg is outside the scope, or that has lost its pair, moves the pools as a DEPOSIT or a WITHDRAWAL of its amount: arriving, it first restores withdrawn returns from \(W\) into \(R_b\) and the rest is \(K_b\); leaving, it takes \(K_b\) first, then \(R_b\), which goes to \(W\) (example E).
  • An exchange result on cash a broker holds in another currency goes to \(R_b\); a loss larger than \(R_b\) comes out of \(K_b\), as a FEE does. \(\mathrm{CapitalBaseline}\) does not move (Portfolio Engine — §6).

🔗 Full per-broker update rules: Portfolio Engine — §6 Three-Pool Model

docs.text:
One broker, report currency EUR, rates in EUR per USD; \(\varepsilon\) is the exchange result on cash.

Step Event \(\varepsilon\) \(K\) \(R\) Cash TotalPnL 1 DEPOSIT 1,000 USD at 0.90 — 900 0 900 0 2 Rate rises to 0.95 +50 900 50 950 +50 3 Rate falls to 0.85 (\(R\) = 50 − 100, \(K\) absorbs −50) −100 850 0 850 −50 4 BUY for 1,000 USD at 0.85 (€850) — 0 0 0 MV − 900

The CapitalBaseline stays €900 throughout: the exchange results are profit and loss, not capital. After step 4, TotalPnL is the security's market value MV less the €900 deposited — −50 on the purchase day if MV equals the €850 paid.

docs.text:
The view of broker \(B\) alone; broker \(A\) is outside it, so each cash transfer between them is an external flow of the view, as in Filtered Views above.

Step Tx at \(B\) \(K\) \(R\) \(W\) Cash 1 DEPOSIT €100, INTEREST €100 100 100 0 200 2 CASH_TRANSFER €150 to \(A\), as a WITHDRAWAL (K=100→0, R=100→50, W+=50) 0 50 50 50 3 CASH_TRANSFER €100 from \(A\), as a DEPOSIT (restore min(100,W=50)=50, the other 50 to K) 50 100 0 150 4 BUY €100 (R first) 50 0 0 50

The purchase of step 4 is all reinvested returns, none of it new capital. The same holds for a transfer leg that has lost its pair, in every view. In the view of \(A\) and \(B\) together, both transfers are internal pairs instead and move the pools from one broker to the other, without touching \(W\).

docs.title: ⚙️ Implementation
docs.text:
The 3-pool model runs in a single per-transaction loop (event-driven, not daily-delta):

  1. Take the transaction's step of its position's average-cost pool, computed before the replay — for a SELL, the cost it removes (\(C\) = pre-sale WAC × quantity sold, at historical rates)
  2. Update K/R/W per transaction type rules, with that \(C\) for a SELL

On each day the exchange rate of a foreign currency held as cash changes, each broker's exchange result on that cash is also booked into its pools, after the day's cash movements and before the day's transactions (§6).

The ROI/TWRR/MWRR input series is derived from day-over-day changes in cumulative_external_cash_flow, the capital baseline. It is not derived from the cash-only external_cash_flow field.

🔗 See Portfolio Engine — §6 for all formal rules.
